Every year, the dependence of optical imaging and holography on computational methods is increasing significantly to the extent that optical methods and components are being completely and efficiently replaced with computational methods at low cost. This roadmap reviews the current scenario in four major areas namely incoherent digital holography, quantitative phase imaging, imaging through scattering layers, and super-resolution imaging. In addition to registering the perspectives of the modern-day architects of the above research areas, the roadmap also reports some of the latest studies on the topic. Computational codes and pseudocodes are presented for computational methods in a plug-and-play fashion for readers to not only read and understand but also practice the latest algorithms with their data. We believe that this roadmap will be a valuable tool for analyzing the current trends in computational methods to predict and prepare the future of computational methods in optical imaging and holography.</p><sec><title>Supplementary Information</title><p>The online version contains supplementary material available at 2024</meta-value></custom-meta></custom-meta-group></article-meta></front><body><sec id="Sec1"><title>Introduction (Joseph Rosen and Vijayakumar Anand)</title><p id="Par2">Light is a powerful means that enables imprinting and recording of the characteristics of objects in real-time on a rewritable mold. The different properties of light, such as intensity and phase distributions, polarization and spectrum allow us to sense the reflectivity and thickness distributions and the birefringence and spectral absorption characteristics of objects [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR1">1</xref>]. When light interacts with an object, the different characteristics of the object are imprinted on those of light, and the goal is to measure the changes in the characteristics of light after the interaction with high accuracy, at a low cost, with fewer resources and in a short time. In the past, the abovementioned measurements involved only optical techniques and optical and recording elements [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR2">2</xref>–<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR10">10</xref>]. However, the invention of charge-coupled devices, computers, and associated computational techniques revolutionized light-based measurement technologies by sharing the responsibilities between optics and computation. The phenomenal work of several researchers resulted in the gradual introduction of computational methods to imaging and holography [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR11">11</xref>–<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR15">15</xref>]. This optical-computational association gradually reached several milestones in imaging technology in the following stages. The first imaging approaches were free of computational methods and completely relied on optical elements and recording media. The introduction of computational methods to imaging and holography shifted the full dependency on optics to both partial ones between optics and computation. Today, the field of imaging relies significantly more on computations than on optical elements, with some techniques even free of optical elements [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR16">16</xref>–<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR20">20</xref>]. With the development of deep learning methods, new possibilities in imaging technology have arisen [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR20">20</xref>]. The entire imaging process in imaging systems that comprises many optical elements, if broken down into individual steps, reveals several closely knitted computational methods and processes with very few optical methods and processes.</p><p id="Par3">The above evolution leads to an important question: what is the next step in this evolutionary process? This question is not direct or easy to answer. To answer this question, it is necessary to review the current state-of-the-art imaging technologies used in all associated sub-fields, such as computational imaging, quantitative phase imaging, quantum imaging, incoherent imaging, imaging through scattering layers, deep learning and polarization imaging. This roadmap is a collection of some of the widely used computational techniques that assist, improve, and replace optical counterparts in today’s imaging technologies. Unlike other roadmaps, this roadmap focuses on computational methods. The roadmap comprises computational techniques developed by some of the leading research groups that include prominent researchers and architects of modern-day computational imaging technologies. In the past, even today, the goal has been to measure the characteristics of an object, such as intensity, phase, and polarization, using light as a real-time mold, but better and faster, with fewer resources and at a low cost. Although it is impossible to cover the entire domain of imaging technology, this roadmap aims to provide insight into some of the latest computational techniques used in advanced imaging technologies. Mini summaries of the computational optical techniques with associated supplementary materials as computational codes are presented in the subsequent sections.</p></sec><sec id="Sec2"><title>Incoherent digital holography with phase-shifting interferometry (Tatsuki Tahara)</title><sec id="Sec3"><title>Background</title><p id="Par4">Digital holography (DH) [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR21">21</xref>–<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR25">25</xref>] is a technique used to record an interference fringe image of the light wave diffracted from an object, termed hologram, and to reconstruct a three-dimensional (3D) image of the object. A laser light source is generally adopted to obtain interference fringes with high visibility. However, a digital hologram of daily-use light is obtained by exploiting incoherent digital holography [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR26">26</xref>–<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR30">30</xref>]. Using incoherent digital holography (IDH), a speckleless holographic 3D image of the object is obtained. Single-pixel holographic fluorescence microscopy [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR31">31</xref>], lensless 3D imaging [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR32">32</xref>], the improvement of the point spread function (PSF) in the in-plane direction [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR33">33</xref>], and full-color 3D imaging with sunlight [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR34">34</xref>] were experimentally demonstrated. In IDH, phase-shifting interferometry (PSI) [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR35">35</xref>] and a common-path in-line configuration are frequently adopted to obtain a clear holographic 3D image of the object and robustness against external vibrations. I introduce IDH techniques using PSI in this section.</p></sec><sec id="Sec4"><title>Methodology</title><p id="Par5">Figure <xref rid="Fig1" ref-type="fig">1</xref> illustrates the schematic of the phase-shifting IDH (PS-IDH) and configurations of frequently adopted optical systems. An object wave generated with spatially incoherent light is diffracted from an object. In IDH, self-interference phenomenon is applied to generate an incoherent hologram from spatially incoherent light. Optical elements for generating two object waves whose wavefront curvature radii are different are set to obtain a self-interference hologram as shown in Fig. <xref rid="Fig1" ref-type="fig">1</xref>a. A phase modulator is set to shift the phase of one of the object waves, and an image sensor records multiple phase-shifted incoherent digital holograms. The complex amplitude distribution in the hologram is retrieved by PSI, and the 3D information of the object is reconstructed by calculating diffraction integrals to the complex amplitude distribution. In PS-IDH, optical setups of the Fresnel incoherent correlation holography (FINCH) type [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR26">26</xref>, <xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR28">28</xref>, <xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR36">36</xref>], conoscopic holography type [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR37">37</xref>, <xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR38">38</xref>], two-arm interferometer type [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR34">34</xref>], optical scanning holography type [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR39">39</xref>–<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR41">41</xref>], and two polarization-sensitive phase-only spatial light modulators (TPP-SLMs) type [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR42">42</xref>, <xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR43">43</xref>] have been proposed. In a FINCH-type optical setup shown in Fig. <xref rid="Fig1" ref-type="fig">1</xref>b, a liquid crystal (LC) SLM works as both a two-wave generator and a phase modulator for obtaining self-interference phase-shifted incoherent holograms. In FINCH, phase-shifted Fresnel phase-lens patterns are displayed, and phase-shifted incoherent holograms are recorded. Polarizers are frequently set to improve the visibility of interference fringes. In a conoscopic-holography-type optical setup shown in Fig. <xref rid="Fig1" ref-type="fig">1</xref>c, instead of an SLM, a solid birefringent material such as calcite is adopted as a polarimetric two-wave generator. In comparison to that of Fig. <xref rid="Fig1" ref-type="fig">1</xref>b, the setup suppresses multi-order diffraction waves when a wide-wavelength-bandwidth light wave illuminates the setup although the size of the setup is enlarged. As another way, IDH is implemented with a classical two-arm interferometer shown in Fig. <xref rid="Fig1" ref-type="fig">1</xref>d and the wavefront curvature radius of one of the two object waves is changed by a concave mirror. Robustness against external vibrations is a current research objective. Figure <xref rid="Fig1" ref-type="fig">1</xref>e is a setup adopting optical scanning holography [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR21">21</xref>, <xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR24">24</xref>, <xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR27">27</xref>] and PSI. Phase shifts are introduced using a phase shifter such as an SLM [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR40">40</xref>, <xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR41">41</xref>] before illuminating an object and phase-shifted Gabor zone plate pattern is illuminated to an object as a structured light. An object is moved along the in-plane direction and a photo detector records a sequence of temporally changed intensity values by introducing phase shifts. The structured light pattern relates the depth position of an object and detected intensity values, and information in the in-plane direction is obtained through optical scanning. Spatially incoherent phase-shifted holograms are numerically generated from the intensity values. The number of pixels and recording speed are dependent on the optical scanning. As described above, PS-IDH systems generally require a polarization filter and/or a half mirror. TPP-SLMs-type optical setup shown in Fig. <xref rid="Fig1" ref-type="fig">1</xref>f does not require these optical elements and is constructed to improve the light-use efficiency. Each SLM displays the phase distribution containing two spherical waves with different wavefront curvature radii based on space-division multiplexing, which is termed spatial multiplexing [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR36">36</xref>]. Phase shifts are introduced to one of the two spherical waves to conduct PSI. By introducing the same phase distributions and phase shifts for respective SLMs, self-interference phase-shifted incoherent holograms are generated. Phase-shifted incoherent holograms for respective polarization directions are formed and multiplexed on the image sensor plane. PS-IDH is implemented when the same phase shifts are introduced for respective polarization directions. It is noted that both 3D and polarization information is simultaneously obtained without a polarization filter by introducing different phase shifts for respective polarization directions and exploiting a holographic multiplexing scheme [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR42">42</xref>, <xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR43">43</xref>]. Single-shot phase shifting (SSPS) [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR44">44</xref>–<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR46">46</xref>] and the computational coherent superposition (CCS) scheme [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR47">47</xref>–<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR49">49</xref>] are combined with these optical setups when conducting single-shot measurement and multidimensional imaging with holographic multiplexing, respectively. CCS is a multidimension-multiplexed PSI technique, and multiple physical quantities such as multiple wavelengths [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR47">47</xref>–<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR49">49</xref>], multiple wavelength bands [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR50">50</xref>], and state of polarization [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR42">42</xref>, <xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR43">43</xref>] are selectively extracted by the signal processing based on PSI. The detailed explanations for PS-IDH with SSPS and CCS are shown in refs. [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR29">29</xref>, <xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR30">30</xref>].<fig id="Fig1" position="float" orientation="portrait"><label>Fig. 1</label><caption><p>Phase-shifting incoherent digital holography (PS-IDH). <bold>a</bold> Schematic. <bold>b</bold> FINCH-type, <bold>c</bold> conoscopic-holography-type, <bold>d</bold> two-arm-interferometer-type, <bold>e</bold> optical-scanning-holography-type, and <bold>f</bold> TPP-SLMs-type optical setups</p></caption><graphic xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" id="MO1" position="float" orientation="portrait" xlink:href="340_2024_8280_Fig1_HTML.jpg"><?image-name 340_2024_8280_Fig1_HTML.jpg?><?image-size 104161?><?image-md5 28a8c4491b36f1cca4061cd02dda130c?><?image-image-server-status LOAD_COMPLETED?><?image-original-height 1126?><?image-original-width 1502?><?image-scaled-height 563?><?image-scaled-width 751?><?image-cloudpmc-urn urn:cdn:blobs/9a7a/11362238/28a8c4491b36/340_2024_8280_Fig1_HTML.jpg?><?thumb-name 340_2024_8280_Fig1_HTML.gif?><?thumb-size 4201?><?thumb-md5 058a39ba16daf901b2ee268963318aeb?><?thumb-image-server-status NEVER_LOAD?><?thumb-scaled-height 79?><?thumb-scaled-width 106?><?thumb-cloudpmc-urn urn:cdn:blobs/9a7a/11362238/058a39ba16da/340_2024_8280_Fig1_HTML.gif?></graphic></fig></p></sec><sec id="Sec5"><title>Results</title><p id="Par6">The TPP-SLMs-type optical setup shown in refs. [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR42">42</xref>, <xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR43">43</xref>] was constructed for experimental demonstrations. PS-IDH with TPP-SLMs is the IDH system with neither linear polarizers nor half mirrors, and a high light-use efficiency is achieved. Experiments on PS-IDH and filter-free polarimetric incoherent holography, termed polarization-filterless polarization-sensitive polarization-multiplexed phase-shifting IDH (P<sup>4</sup>IDH), which is the combination of PS-IDH and CCS, were carried out. Two objects, an origami fan and an origami crane, were set at different depths, and a polarization film was placed in front of the origami fan. The depth difference was 140 mm. The transmission axis of the film was the vertical direction. In this experiment, I set high-resolution LCoS-SLMs [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR51">51</xref>] to display the phase distribution of two spatially multiplexed spherical waves whose focal lengths are 850 mm and infinity. Four holograms in the experiment of PS-IDH and seven holograms in the experiment of P4IDH were obtained with blue LEDs (Thorlabs, LED4D201) whose nominal wavelength and full width at half maximum were 455 nm and 18 nm, respectively. The phase shifts in the horizontal and vertical polarizations of the object wave (θ1, θ2) were (0, 0), (π/2, π/2), (π, π), and (3π/2, 3π/2) in the experiment of PS-IDH and (3π/2, 0), (π, 0), (π/2, 0), (0, 0), (0, π/2), (0, π), and (0, 3π/2) in the experiment of P<sup>4</sup>IDH, respectively. The magnification set by four lenses in the constructed N-shaped self-interference interferometer [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR42">42</xref>, <xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR43">43</xref>] was 0.5 and the field of view for an image hologram in length was 2.66 cm. Figure <xref rid="Fig2" ref-type="fig">2</xref> shows the experimental results. The results indicate that clear 3D image information was reconstructed by PS-IDH and both 3D information and polarization information on the reflective 3D objects were successfully reconstructed without the use of any polarization filter by exploiting P<sup>4</sup>IDH. Depth information is obtained in the numerical refocusing, and quantitative depth-sensing capability is shown. The images of the normalized Stokes parameter S1/S0 shown in Fig. <xref rid="Fig2" ref-type="fig">2</xref>g and h describe quantitative imaging capability of polarimetric information.<fig id="Fig2" position="float" orientation="portrait"><label>Fig. 2</label><caption><p>Experimental results of <bold>a</bold>–<bold>c</bold> PS-IDH and <bold>d</bold>–<bold>h</bold> P<sup>4</sup>IDH. <bold>a</bold> One of the phase-shifted holograms. Reconstructed images numerically focused on <bold>b</bold> origami fan and <bold>c</bold> origami crane. <bold>d </bold>One of the polarization-multiplexed phase-shifted holograms. Reconstructed intensity images numerically focused on <bold>e</bold> origami fan and <bold>f</bold> origami crane. Reconstructed polarimetric images numerically focused on <bold>g</bold> origami fan and <bold>h</bold> origami crane. Blue and red colors in <bold>g</bold> and <bold>h</bold> mean that the normalized Stokes parameter S1/S0 is minus and plus according to the scale bar, respectively. Single-shot 3D imaging [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR52">52</xref>–<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR54">54</xref>] and multidimensional imaging such as multiwavelength-multiplexed 3D imaging [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR55">55</xref>, <xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR56">56</xref>], high-speed 3D motion-picture imaging [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR57">57</xref>], and filter-free polarimetric holographic 3D imaging [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR42">42</xref>, <xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR43">43</xref>] have been experimentally demonstrated, merging SSPS and CCS into PS-IDH. Although single-shot 3D imaging with IDH has also been demonstrated by off-axis configurations [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR26">26</xref>, <xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR58">58</xref>–<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR60">60</xref>], an in-line configuration is frequently adopted in IDH, considering low temporal coherency of daily-use light. Research studies toward filter-free multidimensional motion-picture IDH and real-time measurements, the improvement of specifications such as light-use efficiency and 3D resolution, and developments of promising applications listed in many publications [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR26">26</xref>–<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR30">30</xref>, <xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR42">42</xref>, <xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR43">43</xref>] are listed as future perspectives. The C-codes for generating the multiplexed Fresnel phase lens and phase shifting are given in supplementary materials S1 and S2 respectively.</p></sec></sec><sec id="Sec7"><title>Transport of amplitude into phase using Gerchberg-Saxton algorithm for design of pure phase multifunctional diffractive optical elements (Shivasubramanian Gopinath, Joseph Rosen and Vijayakumar Anand)</title><sec id="Sec8"><title>Background</title><p id="Par8">Multiplexing multiple phase-only diffractive optical functions into a single high-efficiency multifunctional diffractive optical element (DOE) is essential for many applications, such as holography, imaging, and augmented and mixed reality applications [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR61">61</xref>–<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR66">66</xref>]. When multiple phase functions are combined as <inline-formula id="IEq1"><alternatives><tex-math id="M1"><?equation-image-name M1.gif?><?equation-image-status READY?><?equation-image-md5 4def75698e75cdc948310030a8acbe78?><?equation-image-cloudpmc-urn urn:cdn:blobs/9a7a/11362238/4def75698e75/M1.gif?>\documentclass[12pt]{minimal}

However, most of the available modulators, either phase-only or amplitude-only, make the realization of multifunctional diffractive elements challenging. Advanced phase mask design methods and computational optical methods are needed to implement multifunctional DOEs. One of the widely used methods is the random multiplexing (RM) method, where multiple binary random matrices are designed such that the binary states of any mask are mutually exclusive to one another. One unique binary random matrix is assigned to every diffractive function and then summed [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR36">36</xref>]. This RM approach allows the combination of more than two diffractive functions in a single phase-only DOE [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR67">67</xref>]. However, the disadvantages of the RM include scattering noise and low light throughput. The polarization multiplexing (PM) method encodes different diffractive functions to orthogonal polarizations, and consequently, multiplexing more than two functions in a single phase only DOE [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR68">68</xref>] is impossible. Compared to RM, PM has a higher signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) but relatively lower light throughput due to the loss of light at polarizers. In this section, we present a recently developed computational algorithm called Transport of Amplitude into Phase using the Gerchberg Saxton Algorithm (TAP-GSA) for designing multifunctional pure phase DOEs [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR69">69</xref>].</p></sec><sec id="Sec9"><title>Methodology</title><p id="Par9">A schematic of the TAP-GSA is shown in Fig. <xref rid="Fig3" ref-type="fig">3</xref>. This process is iterated until a nonchanging phase matrix is obtained in the mask plane.<fig id="Fig3" position="float" orientation="portrait"><label>Fig. 3</label><caption><p>Schematic of TAP-GSA demonstrated here for multiplexing four diffractive lenses with different focal lengths</p></caption><graphic xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" id="MO3" position="float" orientation="portrait" xlink:href="340_2024_8280_Fig3_HTML.jpg"><?image-name 340_2024_8280_Fig3_HTML.jpg?><?image-size 131863?><?image-md5 8369912ece798e642aa727197511d1ff?><?image-image-server-status LOAD_COMPLETED?><?image-original-height 979?><?image-original-width 1760?><?image-scaled-height 392?><?image-scaled-width 704?><?image-cloudpmc-urn urn:cdn:blobs/9a7a/11362238/8369912ece79/340_2024_8280_Fig3_HTML.jpg?><?thumb-name 340_2024_8280_Fig3_HTML.gif?><?thumb-size 6669?><?thumb-md5 f20966058ec1b82b631a0afbed05f293?><?thumb-image-server-status NEVER_LOAD?><?thumb-scaled-height 80?><?thumb-scaled-width 143?><?thumb-cloudpmc-urn urn:cdn:blobs/9a7a/11362238/f20966058ec1/340_2024_8280_Fig3_HTML.gif?></graphic></fig></p><p id="Par10">In FINCH or IDH, it is necessary to create two different object beams for every object point. In the first versions of FINCH, the generation of two object beams was achieved using a randomly multiplexed diffractive lens, where two diffractive lenses with two different focal lengths are spatially and randomly multiplexed [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR36">36</xref>]. Spatial random multiplexing results in scattering noise, resulting in a low SNR. Polarization multiplexing was then developed by polarizing the input object beam along 45° of the active axis of a birefringent device, resulting in the generation of two different object beams with orthogonal polarizations at the birefringent device [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR33">33</xref>]. A second polarizer was mounted before the image sensor at 45° with respect to the active axis of the birefringent device to cause self-interference. As the SNR improved in polarization multiplexing, the light throughput decreased. TAP-GSA was implemented to design phase masks for FINCH [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR36">36</xref>].</p></sec><sec id="Sec10"><title>Results</title><p id="Par11">The optical configuration of FINCH is shown in Fig. <xref rid="Fig4" ref-type="fig">4</xref>. Light from an incoherently illuminated object is collected and collimated by lens L with a focal length of <italic toggle="yes">f</italic><sub>1</sub> at a distance of <italic toggle="yes">z</italic><sub>1</sub>. The collimated light is modulated by a spatial light modulator (SLM) on which dual diffractive lenses with focal lengths <italic toggle="yes">f</italic><sub>2</sub> = ∞ and <italic toggle="yes">f</italic><sub>3</sub> = <italic toggle="yes">z</italic><sub>2</sub>/2 are displayed, and the holograms are recorded by an image sensor located at a distance of <italic toggle="yes">z</italic><sub>2</sub> from the SLM. The light from every object point is split into two waves that self-interfere to obtain the FINCH hologram. Two polarizers are used one before and one after the SLM for implementing one at a time by the same setup, FINCH with spatial multiplexing using RM, TAP-GSA, at one moment, and polarization multiplexing methods at the other. For RM and TAP-GSA, the multiplexed lenses are displayed with P1 and P2 oriented along the active axis of the SLM. For the PM, P1 and P2 are oriented at 45<sup>o</sup> with respect to the active axis of the SLM, and a single diffractive lens is displayed on the SLM. The experiment was carried out with a high-power LED (Thorlabs, 940 mW, λ = 660 nm and Δλ = 20 nm), SLM (Thorlabs Exulus HD2, 1920 × 1200 pixels, pixel size = 8 μm) and image sensor (Zelux CS165MU/M 1.6 MP monochrome CMOS camera, 1440 × 1080 pixels with pixel size ~ 3.5 µm) with distances z<sub>1</sub> = 5 cm and z<sub>2</sub> = 17.8 cm. The images of the phase masks, FINCH holograms for the three-phase shifts θ = 0, 120, and 240 degrees, magnitude and phase of the complex hologram, and reconstruction results obtained by Fresnel propagation for the RM, TAP-GSA, and PM are shown in Fig. <xref rid="Fig5" ref-type="fig">5</xref>. The average background noise of RM, TAP-GSA, and PM are 3.27 × 10<sup>–3</sup>, 2.32 × 10<sup>–3</sup>, and 0.41 × 10<sup>–3</sup>, respectively. The exposure times needed to achieve the same signal level in the image sensor for RM, TAP-GSA, and PM were 440, 384, and 861 ms, respectively. Comparing all three approaches, TAP-GSA has better light throughput than both RM and PM and has an SNR better than that of RM and close to that of PM.<fig id="Fig4" position="float" orientation="portrait"><label>Fig. 4</label><caption><p>Optical configuration of FINCH</p></caption><graphic xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" id="MO4" position="float" orientation="portrait" xlink:href="340_2024_8280_Fig4_HTML.jpg"><?image-name 340_2024_8280_Fig4_HTML.jpg?><?image-size 47283?><?image-md5 22270aecfc9b39ac5bbbfcb2a40abb61?><?image-image-server-status LOAD_COMPLETED?><?image-original-height 433?><?image-original-width 970?><?image-scaled-height 288?><?image-scaled-width 646?><?image-cloudpmc-urn urn:cdn:blobs/9a7a/11362238/22270aecfc9b/340_2024_8280_Fig4_HTML.jpg?><?thumb-name 340_2024_8280_Fig4_HTML.gif?><?thumb-size 6376?><?thumb-md5 a3062d20ab8ef74a1f1e101af3e0b1f4?><?thumb-image-server-status NEVER_LOAD?><?thumb-scaled-height 80?><?thumb-scaled-width 179?><?thumb-cloudpmc-urn urn:cdn:blobs/9a7a/11362238/a3062d20ab8e/340_2024_8280_Fig4_HTML.gif?></graphic></fig><fig id="Fig5" position="float" orientation="portrait"><label>Fig. 5</label><caption><p>Phase masks and FINCH holograms of the USAF target for <italic toggle="yes">θ</italic> = 0, 120, and 240 degrees, magnitude and phase of the complex hologram and reconstruction result by Fresnel propagation. Rows 1, 2, and 3 are the results for the RM, TAP-GSA, and polarization multiplexing, respectively</p></caption><graphic xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" id="MO5" position="float" orientation="portrait" xlink:href="340_2024_8280_Fig5_HTML.jpg"><?image-name 340_2024_8280_Fig5_HTML.jpg?><?image-size 116594?><?image-md5 0276c4a6e0b9a7fda16d44c40d8674a7?><?image-image-server-status LOAD_COMPLETED?><?image-original-height 750?><?image-original-width 1694?><?image-scaled-height 300?><?image-scaled-width 677?><?image-cloudpmc-urn urn:cdn:blobs/9a7a/11362238/0276c4a6e0b9/340_2024_8280_Fig5_HTML.jpg?><?thumb-name 340_2024_8280_Fig5_HTML.gif?><?thumb-size 10012?><?thumb-md5 06809dfc777ddfe1bb05b38d8f036aa2?><?thumb-image-server-status NEVER_LOAD?><?thumb-scaled-height 80?><?thumb-scaled-width 180?><?thumb-cloudpmc-urn urn:cdn:blobs/9a7a/11362238/06809dfc777d/340_2024_8280_Fig5_HTML.gif?></graphic></fig></p></sec><sec id="Sec11"><title>Conclusion and future perspectives</title><p id="Par12">The useful computational algorithm TAP-GSA was developed to combine multiple phase functions into a single phase-only function. The algorithm has been demonstrated on FINCH to improve both the SNR and the light throughput. We believe that the developed algorithm will benefit many research areas, such as beam shaping, optical trapping, holography and augmented reality. The MATLAB code with comments is provided in the supplementary materials S3.</p></sec></sec><sec id="Sec12"><title>PSF engineering for Fresnel incoherent correlation holography (Francis Gracy Arockiaraj, Saulius Juodkazis and Vijayakumar Anand)</title><sec id="Sec13"><title>Background</title><p id="Par13">In the previous sections, FINCH was implemented based on the principles of IDH with self-interference, three to four camera shots with phase-shifting and reconstruction by back propagation of the complex hologram. FINCH is a linear, shift-invariant system and therefore FINCH can also be implemented based on the principles of coded aperture imaging (CAI). The FINCH hologram for an object is formed by the summation of shifted FINCH point responses. Therefore, if the point spread hologram (<italic toggle="yes">I</italic><sub><italic toggle="yes">PSH</italic></sub>) library is recorded at different depths, then they can be used as reconstruction functions of FINCH object hologram (<italic toggle="yes">I</italic><sub><italic toggle="yes">OH</italic></sub>) at those depths [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR70">70</xref>–<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR77">77</xref>]. This FINCH as CAI replaced the multiple camera recordings by a one-time calibration procedure involving the recording of the <italic toggle="yes">I</italic><sub><italic toggle="yes">PSH</italic></sub> library. However, this approach of FINCH as CAI has the challenges associated with CAI. One of the challenges in the implementation is that the lateral resolution in CAI is governed by the size of the pinhole used for recording the <italic toggle="yes">I</italic><sub><italic toggle="yes">PSH</italic></sub> instead of the numerical aperture (NA) [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR70">70</xref>–<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR79">79</xref>]. It is possible to record the <italic toggle="yes">I</italic><sub><italic toggle="yes">PSH</italic></sub> with a pinhole with a smaller diameter that is close to the lateral resolution limit governed by the NA. But with a smaller aperture, there is lesser number of photons and increased noise. In this section, we present a recently developed PSH engineering technique that allows to improve the reconstructions of FINCH as CAI [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR80">80</xref>].</p></sec><sec id="Sec14"><title>Methodology</title><p id="Par14">The optical configuration of FINCH as CAI using Lucy-Richardson-Rosen algorithm (LRRA) is shown in Fig. <xref rid="Fig6" ref-type="fig">6</xref>a. The light from the object point is split into two beams differently modulated using phase masks created from the TAP-GSA displayed on the SLM, and the two beams are then interfered to form a self-interference hologram. The <italic toggle="yes">I</italic><sub><italic toggle="yes">PSH</italic></sub> and <italic toggle="yes">I</italic><sub><italic toggle="yes">OH</italic></sub> holograms are required to reconstruct object information using the LRRA. In the PSH engineering technique, the <italic toggle="yes">I</italic><sub><italic toggle="yes">PSH</italic></sub> is recorded using a pinhole that can allow sufficient number of photons to record a hologram with minimum detector noise in the first step. In the next step, the ideal PSH <italic toggle="yes">I</italic><sub><italic toggle="yes">IPSH</italic></sub> for a single point is synthesized from the <italic toggle="yes">I</italic><sub><italic toggle="yes">PSH</italic></sub> recorded for the large pinhole and direct image of the pinhole using LRRA. From the results shown in Fig. <xref rid="Fig8" ref-type="fig">8</xref>d–f, it can be seen that the result of PSH engineering has better SNR and more object information compared to the result obtained for a PSH recorded using a large pinhole. <fig id="Fig8" position="float" orientation="portrait"><label>Fig. 8</label><caption><p>Experimental results of FINCH as CAI. <bold>a</bold> FINCH phase mask for DoF 98%, <bold>b</bold> recorded <italic toggle="yes">I</italic><sub><italic toggle="yes">PSH</italic></sub> for 50 μm, <bold>c</bold> Engineered <italic toggle="yes">I</italic><sub><italic toggle="yes">PSH</italic></sub>, <bold>d</bold> reconstruction result of (<bold>b</bold>), <bold>e</bold> reconstruction result of (<bold>c</bold>), <bold>f</bold> direct imaging result</p></caption><graphic xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" id="MO8" position="float" orientation="portrait" xlink:href="340_2024_8280_Fig8_HTML.jpg"><?image-name 340_2024_8280_Fig8_HTML.jpg?><?image-size 160624?><?image-md5 bf8332b81a9fbabed37092f0ee9ac651?><?image-image-server-status LOAD_COMPLETED?><?image-original-height 602?><?image-original-width 965?><?image-scaled-height 401?><?image-scaled-width 643?><?image-cloudpmc-urn urn:cdn:blobs/9a7a/11362238/bf8332b81a9f/340_2024_8280_Fig8_HTML.jpg?><?thumb-name 340_2024_8280_Fig8_HTML.gif?><?thumb-size 10757?><?thumb-md5 8bc8d472200eb97d58dc2d9f9fc75383?><?thumb-image-server-status NEVER_LOAD?><?thumb-scaled-height 80?><?thumb-scaled-width 128?><?thumb-cloudpmc-urn urn:cdn:blobs/9a7a/11362238/8bc8d472200e/340_2024_8280_Fig8_HTML.gif?></graphic></fig></p><sec id="Sec16"><title>Conclusion and future perspectives</title><p id="Par17">The lateral resolution of all imaging systems is governed by the NA of the system. However, in CAI, there is a secondary resolution limit given by the size of the pinhole that is used to record the PSF. This secondary resolution is usually lower than the NA defined lateral resolution. When FINCH is implemented as CAI, the above limitation ruins one of the most important advantages of FINCH which is the super lateral resolution. A PSH engineering method has been developed to shift the resolution limit of CAI back to the limit defined by the NA. A recently developed algorithm LRRA was used for this demonstration. However, the developed PSH engineering method can also work with other reconstruction methods such as non-linear reconstruction [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR81">81</xref>], Weiner deconvolution [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR82">82</xref>] and other advanced non-linear deconvolution methods [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR83">83</xref>]. While the PSH engineering approach improved the reconstruction results, advanced reconstruction methods are needed to minimize the differences in SNR between reconstructions of ideal PSH and synthesized ideal PSH. The PSH engineering method is not limited to FINCH as CAI but can be applied to many CAI methods [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR84">84</xref>]. The MATLAB code for implementing the PSH engineering method using LRRA is given in the supplementary section S4.</p></sec></sec><sec id="Sec17"><title>Single molecule localization from self-interference digital holography (Shaoheng Li and Peter Kner)</title><sec id="Sec18"><title>Background</title><p id="Par18">Single Molecule Localization Microscopy (SMLM) has emerged as a powerful technique for breaking the diffraction limit in optical microscopy, enabling the precise localization—typically to less than 20 nm—of individual fluorescent molecules within biological samples [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR85">85</xref>]. However, the maximum depth of field for 3D-SMLM so far is still limited to a few microns. Self-interference digital holography (SIDH) can reconstruct images over an extended axial range [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR26">26</xref>]. We have proposed combining SIDH with SMLM to perform 3D super-resolution imaging with nanometer precision over a large axial range without mechanical refocusing. Previous work from our group has experimentally demonstrated localization of fluorescent microspheres using SIDH from only a few thousand photons [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR86">86</xref>–<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR88">88</xref>]. SIDH produces a complex hologram from which the full 3D image of the emitter can be recreated. By determining the center of this 3D image, the emitter can be localized. Here, we describe the algorithm for localizing emitters from the SIDH data.</p></sec><sec id="Sec19"><title>Methodology</title><p id="Par19">Three raw images of one or a few emitters are collected with an added phase shifts of 120° introduced between the two arms of the interferometer. The PSH is then calculated using the standard formula which eliminates the background and twin image [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR36">36</xref>]. Then, the 3D PSF of the emitter can be reconstructed with a finer axial step—100 nm for our experiments. For other 3D SMLM techniques, the axial localization is determined by PSF shape or by comparing two different PSF images [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR89">89</xref>, <xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR90">90</xref>]. Because SIDH provides access to the full 3D PSF, the center of emission can be localized in all 3 dimensions using the same approach. The 3D centroid can be calculated, or maximum likelihood estimation can be used to determine the center of a three-dimensional Gaussian approximation to the PSF [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR91">91</xref>]. Here, we localize the center of the PSF by performing two-dimensional curve-fitting. 2D xy and yz slices are cut through the maximum intensity pixel and Gaussian fits are performed. As can be seen from Fig. <xref rid="Fig9" ref-type="fig">9</xref>c, the localization precision is sensitive to the level of background, and we estimate the background level in Fig. <xref rid="Fig9" ref-type="fig">9</xref>e to be 13 photons/pixel.</p></sec><sec id="Sec21"><title>Conclusion and future perspectives</title><p id="Par22">We have demonstrated a straightforward algorithm for the localization of point sources from SIDH images. With low background, SMLM-SIDH can achieve better than 10 nm precision in all three dimensions over an axial range greater than 10 µm. In future work, we will optimize the reconstruction process by extracting the fluorophore position directly from the hologram without explicitly reconstructing the PSF. It should also be possible to capture only one hologram and then discard the twin-image based on image analysis. Future work will also include incorporating aberration correction into the reconstruction process. Single fluorophores emit several hundred to several thousand photons, and we plan to demonstrate localization of single fluorophores. The Python codes for SMLM-SIDH are given in supplementary materials S5 and GitHub [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR92">92</xref>].</p></sec></sec><sec id="Sec22"><title>Deep learning-based illumination and detection correction in light-sheet microscopy (Mani Ratnam Rai, Chen Li and Alon Greenbaum)</title><sec id="Sec23"><title>Background</title><p id="Par23">Light-sheet fluorescence microscopy (LSFM) has become an essential tool in life sciences due to its fast acquisition speed and optical sectioning capability. As such, LFSM is widely employed for imaging large volumes of tissue cleared samples [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR93">93</xref>]. LSFM operates by projecting a thin light sheet into the tissue, exciting fluorophores, and the emitted photons are then collected by a wide-field detection system positioned perpendicular to the illumination axis of the light sheet [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR93">93</xref>, <xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR94">94</xref>]. The quality of LSFM images hinges on the performance of both the illumination and detection aspects of the microscopy system. On the illumination side: challenges arise from the non-coplanar alignment of the illumination beam and the focal plane of the detection lens, resulting in uneven focus across the field of view (FOV) (Fig. <xref rid="Fig10" ref-type="fig">10</xref>a) [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR95">95</xref>]. In the detection side, when imaging deep, the tissue components introduce aberrations into the imaging system, particularly when imaging complex specimens such as cochlea, bones, or whole organisms with transitions from soft to hard tissue (Fig. <xref rid="Fig10" ref-type="fig">10</xref>b) [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR94">94</xref>]. Most researchers tend to address either the illumination or detection errors independently, often neglecting their interconnected nature. In this research, we systematically quantified the correction procedures for both illumination and detection errors. Then, we developed two distinct deep learning methods: one for illumination correction and the other for aberration correction on the detection side. The proposed system is thoughtfully designed to achieve the highest quality 3D imaging without the need for human intervention. <fig id="Fig10" position="float" orientation="portrait"><label>Fig. 10</label><caption><p><bold>a</bold> Illumination and <bold>b</bold> detection errors in LSFM. <bold>c</bold> Experimental schematic for correcting the illumination and detection errors in a custom-LSFM, with a deformable mirror, and two galvo mirrors</p></caption><graphic xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" id="MO10" position="float" orientation="portrait" xlink:href="340_2024_8280_Fig10_HTML.jpg"><?image-name 340_2024_8280_Fig10_HTML.jpg?><?image-size 72331?><?image-md5 8afc93fd3c5915ab4c399a5d74b47ca2?><?image-image-server-status LOAD_COMPLETED?><?image-original-height 886?><?image-original-width 1772?><?image-scaled-height 354?><?image-scaled-width 708?><?image-cloudpmc-urn urn:cdn:blobs/9a7a/11362238/8afc93fd3c59/340_2024_8280_Fig10_HTML.jpg?><?thumb-name 340_2024_8280_Fig10_HTML.gif?><?thumb-size 5806?><?thumb-md5 b28bc88fd00f90384321d839bc5d0c30?><?thumb-image-server-status NEVER_LOAD?><?thumb-scaled-height 80?><?thumb-scaled-width 160?><?thumb-cloudpmc-urn urn:cdn:blobs/9a7a/11362238/b28bc88fd00f/340_2024_8280_Fig10_HTML.gif?></graphic></fig></p></sec><sec id="Sec24"><title>Methodology</title><p id="Par24">The initial phase of our research involved establishing the order for addressing aberrations, namely, whether to correct illumination or detection errors first [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR94">94</xref>]. Following this, two distinct deep learning models were developed: one for rectifying sample induced detection aberrations and the other for addressing illumination errors, simply put, making sure that the illumination beam was parallel and overlapped with the objective detection plane. In the detection network, we employed a 13-layer RESNET-based network, trained and validated on valuable biomedical samples like porcine cochlea and mouse brain [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR96">96</xref>]. During training, data are generated by first correcting aberrations using a classical grid search approach per imaging location. Once the aberrations are corrected, a known aberration is introduced into the non-aberrated images using a deformable mirror (DM), and two defocused images with known aberrations are captured. During the testing phase, the network receives two defocused images as input and estimates coma, astigmatism, and spherical aberrations, and the DM is utilized to correct the aberrations based on the predictions of the network. To correct illumination errors, a U-net-based network was utilized and integrated into our LSFM setup [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR95">95</xref>]. This algorithm captured two defocused images as well, and the images served as input to the deep learning model. The network generated a defocus map. Subsequently, this map is employed to estimate and rectify angular and defocus aberrations through the utilization of two galvo scanners and a linear motorized stage (Fig. <xref rid="Fig10" ref-type="fig">10</xref>c).</p></sec><sec id="Sec25"><title>Results</title><p id="Par25">The experimental demonstration of the proposed work was performed using a custom-built LSFM system (Fig. <xref rid="Fig10" ref-type="fig">10</xref>c). Tissue cleared brains were used to experimentally demonstrate the proposed work. We have found that it is better to first correct the illumination errors and only then the detection aberrations. Figure <xref rid="Fig11" ref-type="fig">11</xref>a shows the image before and after illumination correction. Before the correction, only the top portion of the FOV is in focus whereas after the illumination correction, the entire FOV is in focus as seen in the defocus map. The color bar in Fig. <xref rid="Fig11" ref-type="fig">11</xref>a shows the defocus level. Figure <xref rid="Fig11" ref-type="fig">11</xref>b shows the images before and after correction of detection aberrations.<fig id="Fig11" position="float" orientation="portrait"><label>Fig. 11</label><caption><p><bold>a</bold> Illumination correction in LSFM. <bold>b</bold> Detection correction in LSFM</p></caption><graphic xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" id="MO11" position="float" orientation="portrait" xlink:href="340_2024_8280_Fig11_HTML.jpg"><?image-name 340_2024_8280_Fig11_HTML.jpg?><?image-size 121526?><?image-md5 1c16da10d72edcccbb3d71385bb37aa7?><?image-image-server-status LOAD_COMPLETED?><?image-original-height 852?><?image-original-width 1502?><?image-scaled-height 426?><?image-scaled-width 751?><?image-cloudpmc-urn urn:cdn:blobs/9a7a/11362238/1c16da10d72e/340_2024_8280_Fig11_HTML.jpg?><?thumb-name 340_2024_8280_Fig11_HTML.gif?><?thumb-size 7518?><?thumb-md5 264da4b7c7d9bcb6004d9025abacd6c6?><?thumb-image-server-status NEVER_LOAD?><?thumb-scaled-height 80?><?thumb-scaled-width 141?><?thumb-cloudpmc-urn urn:cdn:blobs/9a7a/11362238/264da4b7c7d9/340_2024_8280_Fig11_HTML.gif?></graphic></fig></p></sec><sec id="Sec26"><title>Conclusion and future perspectives</title><p id="Par26">In this work, we have developed machine learning based method to correct illumination and detection errors in LSFM. The proposed system can estimate errors from two defocused images. The developed technique will be pragmatic in fully automated error free 3D imaging of large tissue samples without any human intervention. The Python codes for Illumination correction and detection correction are given in <ext-link xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" ext-link-type="uri" xlink:href="https://github.com/Chenli235/AngleCorrection_Unet">https://github.com/Chenli235/AngleCorrection_Unet</ext-link> and <ext-link xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" ext-link-type="uri" xlink:href="https://github.com/maniRr/Detection-correction">https://github.com/maniRr/Detection-correction</ext-link> and in supplementary materials S6.</p></sec></sec><sec id="Sec27"><title>Complex amplitude reconstruction of objects above and below the objective focal plane by IHLLS fluorescence microscopy (Christopher Mann, Zack Zurawski, Simon Alford, Jonathan Art, and Mariana Potcoava)</title><sec id="Sec28"><title>Background</title><p id="Par27">The Incoherent Holographic Lattice-Light Sheet (IHLLS) technique, which offers essential volumetric data and is characterized by its high sensitivity and spatio-temporal resolution, contains a diffraction reconstruction package that has been developed into a tool, HOLO_LLS that routinely achieves both lateral and depth resolution, at least micron level [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR28">28</xref>, <xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR97">97</xref>, <xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR98">98</xref>]. The software enables data visualization and serve a multitude of purposes ranging from calibration steps to volumetric imaging of live cells, in which the structure and intracellular milieu is rapidly changing, where phase imaging gives quantitative information on the state and size of subcellular structures [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR98">98</xref>–<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR100">100</xref>]. This work presents a simple experimental and numerical procedures that have been incorporated into a program package to highlight the imaging capabilities of IHLLS detection system. This capability is demonstrated for 200 nm suspension microspheres and the advantages are discussed by comparing holographic reconstructions with images taken by using conventional Lattice-Light Sheet (LLS). Our study introduces the two configurations of this optical design: IHLLS 1L, used for calibration, and IHLLS 2L, used for sample imaging. IHLLS 1L, an incoherent version of the LLS, creates a hologram via a plane wave and a spherical wave using the same scanning geometry as the LLS in dithering mode. Conversely, IHLLS 2L employs a fixed detection microscope objective to create a hologram with two spherical waves, serving as the incoherent LLS version. By modulating the wavefront of the emission beam with two diffractive lenses uploaded on the phase SLM, this system can attain full Field of View (FOV) and deeper scanning depth with fewer z-galvanometric mirror displacements.</p></sec><sec id="Sec29"><title>Methodology</title><p id="Par28">The schematic of the IHLLS detection system is shown in Fig. <xref rid="Fig12" ref-type="fig">12</xref>. The IHLLS system is a home-built extra hardware added to an existing lattice light-sheet instrument. The IHLLS system is composed of two parts which must both operate in order for the system to perform as intended. The z-scanning principle in IHLLS 1L, same as in LLS, is that both the z-galvanometric mirror (zgalvo) and the detection objective (zpiezo), synchronize in motion to scan the sample in 3D, Fig. <xref rid="Fig12" ref-type="fig">12</xref>a. This case is used for calibration purposes, to mimic the conventional LLS but using a diffractive lens of focal length f_SLM [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR36">36</xref>, <xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR101">101</xref>]. In the IHLLS 2L case, two diffractive lenses of finite focal lengths, with non-shared randomly selected pixels, Fig. <xref rid="Fig12" ref-type="fig">12</xref>b, are simultaneously uploaded on the SLM and four phase-shifting intensity images with different phase factors are recorded and saved in the computer sequentially and numerically processed by in-house diffraction software. f<sub>SLM</sub> = 400 mm, f<sub>d1</sub> = 435 mm, f<sub>d2</sub> = 550 mm; here, we chose two focal lengths of size closer to the calibration focal length</p></caption><graphic xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" id="MO13" position="float" orientation="portrait" xlink:href="340_2024_8280_Fig13_HTML.jpg"><?image-name 340_2024_8280_Fig13_HTML.jpg?><?image-size 100144?><?image-md5 fd74d96516913a84a508d847742182a9?><?image-image-server-status LOAD_COMPLETED?><?image-original-height 415?><?image-original-width 965?><?image-scaled-height 277?><?image-scaled-width 643?><?image-cloudpmc-urn urn:cdn:blobs/9a7a/11362238/fd74d9651691/340_2024_8280_Fig13_HTML.jpg?><?thumb-name 340_2024_8280_Fig13_HTML.gif?><?thumb-size 9957?><?thumb-md5 ef547e925cd457c8b2df83e533b5179a?><?thumb-image-server-status NEVER_LOAD?><?thumb-scaled-height 80?><?thumb-scaled-width 186?><?thumb-cloudpmc-urn urn:cdn:blobs/9a7a/11362238/ef547e925cd4/340_2024_8280_Fig13_HTML.gif?></graphic></fig></p></sec><sec id="Sec30"><title>Results</title><p id="Par29">In this work, we show how to numerically compute IHLLS diffraction patterns with the HOLO_LLS package. The entire package is implemented in MATLAB or Python. Here, we present the MATLAB version. We split the reconstruction process into four steps to produce numerical approximation of the full electric field (amplitude and phase) of the object: (a) addition of all complex fields built by phase shifting holography (PSH) at various z_galvo positions to create a bigger field; (b) apply parameter optimization to the complex wave hologram, a real-space bandpass filter that suppresses the pixel noise while retaining information of a characteristic size, (c) reconstruct the object data from the hologram (backpropagate), and (d) 3D volume representation from the obtained object data. The diffraction subroutine uses the Angular Spectrum Method as the Fresnel and Fraunhofer regimes are limited by the requirement of a different grid scale and by certain approximations [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR102">102</xref>]. As an example of the methods explained, we present MATLAB pseudocodes for making diffractive lenses and for the 3D volume reconstruction from phase-shift holographic images. We hope this software improves the reproducibility of research, thus enabling consistent comparison of data between research groups and the quality of specific numerical reconstructions. The recorded intensity distributions, amplitude and phase after Fresnel propagation and reconstruction results for different scanning positions of z-galvo mirror from 40 µm to −  40 µm in steps of 10 µm are shown in Fig. <xref rid="Fig14" ref-type="fig">14</xref>.<fig id="Fig14" position="float" orientation="portrait"><label>Fig. 14</label><caption><p><bold>a</bold> Z-galvo scanning locations. <bold>b</bold> IHLLS – 2L intensity images at θ = 0. <bold>c</bold> Amplitude and phase obtained by Angular Spectrum propagation method. <bold>d</bold> Holographic reconstruction</p></caption><graphic xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" id="MO14" position="float" orientation="portrait" xlink:href="340_2024_8280_Fig14_HTML.jpg"><?image-name 340_2024_8280_Fig14_HTML.jpg?><?image-size 90792?><?image-md5 4bf03ae281eef33736d6f333409b947d?><?image-image-server-status LOAD_COMPLETED?><?image-original-height 920?><?image-original-width 1832?><?image-scaled-height 368?><?image-scaled-width 732?><?image-cloudpmc-urn urn:cdn:blobs/9a7a/11362238/4bf03ae281ee/340_2024_8280_Fig14_HTML.jpg?><?thumb-name 340_2024_8280_Fig14_HTML.gif?><?thumb-size 7078?><?thumb-md5 508a8a43e846f3d04965af9d5f5ff3f1?><?thumb-image-server-status NEVER_LOAD?><?thumb-scaled-height 80?><?thumb-scaled-width 159?><?thumb-cloudpmc-urn urn:cdn:blobs/9a7a/11362238/508a8a43e846/340_2024_8280_Fig14_HTML.gif?></graphic></fig></p></sec><sec id="Sec31"><title>Conclusion and future perspectives</title><p id="Par30">Our approach will enable automated capture of complex data volumes over time to achieve spatial and temporal resolutions to track dynamic movements of cellular structure in 3D over time. It will enable high temporal resolution of the spatial relationships between cellular structures and retain both amplitude and phase information in the reconstructed images. We have theoretically and practically demonstrated the feasibility of the approach to provide a working microscope system. Our next steps will automate 3D scanning and IHLLS 2L imaging in multiple wavelengths by sweeping excitation through hundreds of z-axis planes. We will then fully automate reconstruction software. Our overall goals are to integrate phase image acquisition in multiple z planes and excitation wavelengths into the existing SPIM software suite. The MATLAB pseudocodes for the HOLO_LLS are provided in the supplementary materials S7.</p></sec></sec><sec id="Sec32"><title>Sparse-view computed tomography for passive two-dimensional ultrafast imaging (Yingming Lai and Jinyang Liang)</title><sec id="Sec33"><title>Background</title><p id="Par31">Sparse-view computed tomography (SV-CT) is an advanced computational method to obtain the three-dimensional (3D) internal spatial structure [i.e., (<italic toggle="yes">x</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">y</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">z</italic>)] of an object from a few angle-diverse projections [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR103">103</xref>]. Compared with traditional CT, SV-CT effectively reduces acquisition time with minimally compromising imaging quality. Since its invention, SV-CT has been prominently applied scenarios such as in x-ray medical imaging and industrial product testing scenarios to reduce the radiation dose received by patients and samples [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR104">104</xref>–<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR106">106</xref>]. In recent years, SV-CT has begun to be noticed as an advanced imaging strategy for efficiently recording spatiotemporal information [i.e., (<italic toggle="yes">x</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">y</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">t</italic>)] [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR107">107</xref>, <xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR108">108</xref>]. Despite enabling ultrafast imaging speeds, these techniques are based on active laser illumination, making them unsuitable for self-illumination and color-selective dynamic scenes. In this chapter, we present a newly developed compressed ultrafast tomographic imaging (CUTI) method by applying SV-CT to the spatiotemporal domain with passive projections.</p></sec><sec id="Sec34"><title>Methodology</title><p id="Par32">CUTI achieves spatiotemporal SV-CT based on streak imaging whose typical configuration includes three parts: an imaging unit, a temporal shearing unit, and a two-dimensional (2D) detector. As shown in Fig. <xref rid="Fig15" ref-type="fig">15</xref>, after being imaged by the imaging unit, the dynamic scene <italic toggle="yes">I</italic>(<italic toggle="yes">x</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">y</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">t</italic>) is deflected to different spatial positions on the detector by the temporal shearing unit [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR109">109</xref>].
