				\begin{document}$${\Phi }_{\text{TV}}(\cdot )$$\end{document}</tex-math><mml:math xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" id="M148"><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mi mathvariant="normal">Φ</mml:mi><mml:mtext>TV</mml:mtext></mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo><mml:mo>·</mml:mo><mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mrow></mml:math><inline-graphic xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" xlink:href="340_2024_8280_Article_IEq71.gif"><?image-name 340_2024_8280_Article_IEq71.gif?><?image-size 314?><?image-md5 c753cc4a38a1ce6dee104a99726f4447?><?image-image-server-status NEVER_LOAD?><?image-scaled-height 19?><?image-scaled-width 48?><?image-cloudpmc-urn urn:cdn:blobs/9a7a/11362238/c753cc4a38a1/340_2024_8280_Article_IEq71.gif?><?thumb-name 340_2024_8280_Article_IEq71.gif?><?thumb-size 314?><?thumb-md5 c753cc4a38a1ce6dee104a99726f4447?><?thumb-image-server-status NEVER_LOAD?><?thumb-scaled-height 19?><?thumb-scaled-width 48?><?thumb-cloudpmc-urn urn:cdn:blobs/9a7a/11362238/c753cc4a38a1/340_2024_8280_Article_IEq71.gif?></inline-graphic></alternatives></inline-formula> is the 3D total-variation regularization function [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR112">112</xref>].</p></sec><sec id="Sec35"><title>Results</title><p id="Par37">The performance of CUTI was demonstrated using an image-converter streak camera to capture an ultrafast ultraviolet (UV) dynamic event [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR110">110</xref>]. Figure <xref rid="Fig16" ref-type="fig">16</xref>a illustrates the generation of two spatially and temporally separated 266-nm, 100-fs laser pulses via a Michelson interferometer, with a 1.6-ns time delay introduced between them. These pulses undergo modulation by a resolution target as shown in the inset of Fig. <xref rid="Fig16" ref-type="fig">16</xref>a. Subsequently, 11 spatiotemporal projections were acquired within the angular range <italic toggle="yes">θ</italic><sub><italic toggle="yes">i</italic></sub> ∈ [− 45°, + 45°] employing a 9° angular step. By setting the regularization parameter to <italic toggle="yes">τ</italic> = 0.0204, the event was successfully reconstructed using the TTR algorithm at an imaging speed of 0.5 trillion (0.5 × 10<sup>12</sup>) frames per second. Figure <xref rid="Fig16" ref-type="fig">16</xref>b represents six representative frames in the reconstruction of the two pulses. To quantitatively assess the image quality, selected cross-sections were extracted at the first pulse (at 150 ps) and the second pulse (at 1746 ps). These results were compared with the reference image captured without temporal shearing (Fig. <xref rid="Fig16" ref-type="fig">16</xref>c, d). Using a 10% contrast threshold, at <italic toggle="yes">t</italic> = 150 ps, the spatial resolutions were determined as 15.6 and 14.1 lp/mm in the <italic toggle="yes">x</italic>- and <italic toggle="yes">y</italic>-directions, respectively. At <italic toggle="yes">t</italic> = 1746 ps, the values were 13.2 and 14.1 lp/mm. Figure <xref rid="Fig16" ref-type="fig">16</xref>e shows the reconstructed temporal trace of this event. <fig id="Fig16" position="float" orientation="portrait"><label>Fig. 16</label><caption><p>Capture two spatially and temporally separated UV pulses by implementing CUTI to a standard UV streak camera. <bold>a</bold> Experimental setup. M1 − M2: mirrors. Magenta-boxed inset: the reference image was captured without using temporal shearing. <bold>b</bold> Representative frames of the reconstruction scenes. <bold>c</bold> Selected cross-sections of the resolution target in the <italic toggle="yes">x</italic>- and <italic toggle="yes">y</italic>-direction at <italic toggle="yes">t</italic> = 150 ps. (<bold>d</bold>) As (<bold>c</bold>), but shows the profiles <italic toggle="yes">t</italic> = 1746 ps. <bold>e</bold> Temporal trace of the reconstruction. <italic toggle="yes">FWHM</italic> full width at half maximum. Adapted with permission from Ref. [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR110">110</xref>]</p></caption><graphic xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" id="MO16" position="float" orientation="portrait" xlink:href="340_2024_8280_Fig16_HTML.jpg"><?image-name 340_2024_8280_Fig16_HTML.jpg?><?image-size 116836?><?image-md5 2aae6423c04bb1ac1e2ae84562cbc856?><?image-image-server-status LOAD_COMPLETED?><?image-original-height 1294?><?image-original-width 1662?><?image-scaled-height 517?><?image-scaled-width 664?><?image-cloudpmc-urn urn:cdn:blobs/9a7a/11362238/2aae6423c04b/340_2024_8280_Fig16_HTML.jpg?><?thumb-name 340_2024_8280_Fig16_HTML.gif?><?thumb-size 4978?><?thumb-md5 fdd3545d789ad435633db088a003ff75?><?thumb-image-server-status NEVER_LOAD?><?thumb-scaled-height 79?><?thumb-scaled-width 102?><?thumb-cloudpmc-urn urn:cdn:blobs/9a7a/11362238/fdd3545d789a/340_2024_8280_Fig16_HTML.gif?></graphic></fig></p></sec><sec id="Sec36"><title>Conclusion</title><p id="Par38">As a new computational ultrafast imaging method, CUTI grafts SV-CT to the spatiotemporal domain. The method has been demonstrated in a standard image-converter streak camera for passively capturing an ultrafast UV dynamic event. In the future, CUTI’s image quality can be improved by using an image rotation unit for a larger angular range [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR113">113</xref>] and adopting advanced SV-CT algorithms [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR114">114</xref>, <xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR115">115</xref>]. CUTI is expected to contribute to the observation of many significant transient phenomena [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR116">116</xref>, <xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR117">117</xref>].</p></sec></sec><sec id="Sec37"><title>Computational reconstruction of quantum objects by a modal approach (Fazilah Nothlawala, Chané Moodley and Andrew Forbes)</title><sec id="Sec38"><title>Background</title><p id="Par39">Optical imaging and holography have traditionally been based on exploiting correlations in space, for instance, using position or pixels as the basis on which to measure. Subsequently, structured illumination with computational reconstruction [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR118">118</xref>] has exploited the orthogonality in random and Walsh-Hadamard masks, implemented for high-quality 3D reconstruction of classical objects [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR119">119</xref>] as well as complex amplitude (amplitude and phase) reconstruction of quantum objects [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR120">120</xref>]. Recently, a modal approach has been suggested to enhance the resolution in imaging [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR121">121</xref>], taking the well-known ability to modally resolve optical fields for their full reconstruction [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR122">122</xref>] to that of physical and digital objects. This has been used to infer step heights with nanometer resolution [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR123">123</xref>], to resolve quantum objects [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR124">124</xref>], in quantum metrology [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR125">125</xref>], in phase imaging [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR126">126</xref>] and suggested as a means of searching for exoplanets [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR127">127</xref>]. Here, we will apply it to reconstruct quantum images of complex objects and compare it to conventional quantum computational approaches.</p></sec><sec id="Sec39"><title>Methodology</title><p id="Par40">The idea is very simple: any complete and orthonormal basis can be used to reconstruct a function, and this function can represent a physical or digital object. In the present context it is the image of the object. This is depicted graphically in Fig. <xref rid="Fig17" ref-type="fig">17</xref>a evolving from a pixel basis (top), to a random basis (middle) and finally to a modal basis (bottom). In the case of the latter, the modal function must be chosen with some care to minimize the number of terms in the sum.<fig id="Fig17" position="float" orientation="portrait"><label>Fig. 17</label><caption><p><bold>a</bold> An object can be reconstructed using any complete and orthonormal basis. Three different bases are depicted in this figure: the pixel basis, random basis and a modal basis, respectively. <bold>b</bold> Simple schematic of the experiment where two entangled photons are produced from a nonlinear crystal, one directed to the object and the other to the mask that displays the basis projections. <bold>c</bold> Computational reconstructions of a cat using four mask options</p></caption><graphic xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" id="MO17" position="float" orientation="portrait" xlink:href="340_2024_8280_Fig17_HTML.jpg"><?image-name 340_2024_8280_Fig17_HTML.jpg?><?image-size 69967?><?image-md5 4f791b028435bac8142f799149e4c5b8?><?image-image-server-status LOAD_COMPLETED?><?image-original-height 815?><?image-original-width 1698?><?image-scaled-height 326?><?image-scaled-width 679?><?image-cloudpmc-urn urn:cdn:blobs/9a7a/11362238/4f791b028435/340_2024_8280_Fig17_HTML.jpg?><?thumb-name 340_2024_8280_Fig17_HTML.gif?><?thumb-size 7758?><?thumb-md5 404c0fd1d017c5d9f6194431b82d0e8d?><?thumb-image-server-status NEVER_LOAD?><?thumb-scaled-height 80?><?thumb-scaled-width 166?><?thumb-cloudpmc-urn urn:cdn:blobs/9a7a/11362238/404c0fd1d017/340_2024_8280_Fig17_HTML.gif?></graphic></fig></p><p id="Par41">Because the right hand side can include modal phases, any physical property of the left hand side can be inferred, including full phase retrieval. We do exactly this for the recognition of quantum and classical objects using the experimental set-up shown in Fig. <xref rid="Fig17" ref-type="fig">17</xref>b. Two entangled photons are produced by spontaneous parametric downconversion (SPDC) in a nonlinear crystal and relay imaged from the crystal plane to the object plane in one arm, and to the image plane in the other arm, the latter with a spatial light modulator as a modal analyzer. Thereafter, each photon is collected by optical fibre and detected by single photon avalanche photodiodes (APDs). The spatial light modulator in the imaging arm is used to display digital match filters for each mode in the basis, while the single mode fibre collection performs an optical inner product to return the modal weights. The intra-modal phase is determined by displaying a superposition of modal elements, two of which (sine and cosine) allow the phase to be known unambiguously. All three measurements together (one for amplitude and two for phase) return the complex weighting coefficient. The final image is then computationally reconstructed by adding the terms on the right hand side with the correct complex weights. The process can be augmented by machine learning and artificial intelligence tools to speed up the reconstruction (with fewer projections) and/or to enhance the final image quality. A simulation of the experiment was performed with computational images of a “cat” object shown in Fig. <xref rid="Fig17" ref-type="fig">17</xref>c for four bases.</p></sec><sec id="Sec40"><title>Results</title><p id="Par42">To illustrate how this approach can be used for quantum objects, we use test cases of (I) an amplitude step and checkerboard pattern object, and (II) a phase step object and checkerboard pattern object for both the Walsh-Hadamard and HG mode reconstructions, with experimental images shown in Fig. <xref rid="Fig18" ref-type="fig">18</xref>a and b. The outer area of the dashed white circle for each reconstruction represents the region where noise was suppressed due to lack of SPDC signal. We see the reconstructed images of both the amplitude and phase objects show a high fidelity with both reconstruction approaches (Walsh-Hadamard and HG modes), however the phase objects show a higher object-image fidelity overall. Figure <xref rid="Fig18" ref-type="fig">18</xref>c and d provide a quantitative comparison between the object (simulated reconstructed) and the image through a cross-section, showing good agreement between the object (simulated reconstruction) and the experimental reconstructions for both the Hadamard (blue) and Hermite-Gauss (red) amplitude and phase steps, albeit with a low level of noise, characteristic to quantum experiments, present.<fig id="Fig18" position="float" orientation="portrait"><label>Fig. 18</label><caption><p><bold>a</bold> Amplitude and <bold>b</bold> phase reconstructions for a checkerboard pattern and a step object (shown as insets), using Hermite-Gauss (HG) and Walsh-Hadamard masks. The outer area of the dashed white circle represents the region where noise was suppressed due to lack of SPDC signal. 2D cross-sectional plots of the <bold>c</bold> amplitude and <bold>d</bold> phase step functions with the object (simulation), and reconstructions with the Walsh-Hadamard (blue diamonds) and HG (red dots) masks</p></caption><graphic xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" id="MO18" position="float" orientation="portrait" xlink:href="340_2024_8280_Fig18_HTML.jpg"><?image-name 340_2024_8280_Fig18_HTML.jpg?><?image-size 103357?><?image-md5 4a9b2c05eeb75513a160b9c03b5ba988?><?image-image-server-status LOAD_COMPLETED?><?image-original-height 1026?><?image-original-width 1501?><?image-scaled-height 513?><?image-scaled-width 750?><?image-cloudpmc-urn urn:cdn:blobs/9a7a/11362238/4a9b2c05eeb7/340_2024_8280_Fig18_HTML.jpg?><?thumb-name 340_2024_8280_Fig18_HTML.gif?><?thumb-size 4684?><?thumb-md5 5ef4dd8468bd190580b21a747fe6bb44?><?thumb-image-server-status NEVER_LOAD?><?thumb-scaled-height 80?><?thumb-scaled-width 117?><?thumb-cloudpmc-urn urn:cdn:blobs/9a7a/11362238/5ef4dd8468bd/340_2024_8280_Fig18_HTML.gif?></graphic></fig></p></sec><sec id="Sec41"><title>Conclusion and future perspectives</title><p id="Par43">While scanning methods employing the pixel, Walsh-Hadamard and random bases depend directly on the number of pixels required within the image, the modal approach proves beneficial in that there is no direct correlation between the number of scans required and image resolution. The resolution is set by the optical system itself, while the number of modes required to image the object is dependent on the complexity of the object. The modal approach requires a judicious choice of modal basis as well as the number of terms required to image the object. The introduction of phase only and amplitude only scanning through a modal approach allows for the ability to probe individual properties of an unknown object. The future prospects for computational methods in optical imaging and holography are highly promising, with trends indicating integration of AI for enhanced image reconstruction, the advancement of 3D holography with improved resolution, and the potential impact of quantum techniques. These developments will benefit various fields, including bio-photonics, material science, and quantum cryptography. The introduction of quantum computing and interdisciplinary collaborations will likely act as a catalyst for innovation, expanding the applications and accessibility of optical imaging and holography across industrial and research domains.</p></sec></sec><sec id="Sec42"><title>Label-free sensing of bacteria and viruses using holography and deep learning (Yuzhu Li, Bijie Bai and Aydogan Ozcan)</title><sec id="Sec43"><title>Background</title><p id="Par44">Microorganisms, like bacteria and viruses, play an indispensable role in our ecosystem. While they serve crucial functions, such as facilitating the decomposition of organic waste and signaling environmental changes, certain microorganisms are pathogenic and can lead to diseases like anthrax, tuberculosis, influenza, etc. [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR128">128</xref>]. The replication of bacteria and viruses can be detected using culture-based methods [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR129">129</xref>] and viral plaque assays [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR130">130</xref>], respectively. Though these culture-based methods have the unique ability to identify live and infectious/replicating bacteria and viruses, they are notably time-consuming. Specifically, it usually requires > 24 h for bacterial colonies to form [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR129">129</xref>] and > 2 days for viral plaques [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR131">131</xref>] to grow to sizes discernible to the naked eye. In addition, these methods are labor-intensive, and are subject to human counting errors, as experts/microbiologists need to manually count the number of colony-forming units (CFUs) or plaque-forming units (PFUs) within the test plates after the corresponding incubation period to determine the sample concentrations. Therefore, a more rapid and automated method for detecting the replication of bacteria and viruses is urgently needed.</p><p id="Par45">The combination of time-lapse holographic imaging and deep learning algorithms provides a promising solution to circumvent these limitations. Holographic imaging, regarded as a prominent label-free imaging modality, is effective at revealing features of transparent biological specimens by exploiting the refractive index as an endogenous imaging contrast [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR17">17</xref>, <xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR132">132</xref>]. Consequently, it can be employed to monitor the growth of colonies or viral plaques during their incubation process in a label-free manner. This allows for the capture of subtle spatio-temporal changes associated with colony or viral plaque growth, enabling early detection of them when they are imperceptible to human eye. However, the presence of other potential artifacts (e.g., bubbles, dust, and other random features created by the uncontrolled motion of the sample surface) can hinder the accurate detection of true bacterial colonies or viral plaques. To mitigate such false positive events, deep learning algorithms become critical in automatically differentiating these randomly appearing artifacts from true positive events by leveraging the unique spatio-temporal features of CFU or PFU growth. In this chapter, we will present how the integration of time-lapse holographic imaging and deep learning enables the early detection of bacterial colonies or viral plaques in an automated and label-free manner, achieving significant time savings compared to the gold-standard methods [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR133">133</xref>–<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR135">135</xref>].</p></sec><sec id="Sec44"><title>Methodology</title><p id="Par46">The primary workflow for detecting CFUs and PFUs using holography and deep learning includes key steps such as time-lapse hologram acquisition of test well plates, digital holographic reconstruction, image processing, and deep learning-based CFU/PFU identification and automatic counting, as illustrated in Fig. <xref rid="Fig19" ref-type="fig">19</xref>. The specific methodologies employed in each step differ for CFU and PFU detection, as detailed below.<fig id="Fig19" position="float" orientation="portrait"><label>Fig. 19</label><caption><p>Workflows used for label-free sensing of bacteria (CFUs) and viruses (PFUs) using time-lapse holographic imaging and deep learning. <bold>a</bold> Workflow for CFU early detection using holography and deep learning. <bold>b</bold> Workflow for PFU early detection using holography and deep learning</p></caption><graphic xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" id="MO19" position="float" orientation="portrait" xlink:href="340_2024_8280_Fig19_HTML.jpg"><?image-name 340_2024_8280_Fig19_HTML.jpg?><?image-size 118637?><?image-md5 56b102df7f5a6fa0ad3cc262158e2fef?><?image-image-server-status LOAD_COMPLETED?><?image-original-height 722?><?image-original-width 1946?><?image-scaled-height 289?><?image-scaled-width 778?><?image-cloudpmc-urn urn:cdn:blobs/9a7a/11362238/56b102df7f5a/340_2024_8280_Fig19_HTML.jpg?><?thumb-name 340_2024_8280_Fig19_HTML.gif?><?thumb-size 9178?><?thumb-md5 aedf23fe8b9b2c0c8c982f427283e644?><?thumb-image-server-status NEVER_LOAD?><?thumb-scaled-height 74?><?thumb-scaled-width 200?><?thumb-cloudpmc-urn urn:cdn:blobs/9a7a/11362238/aedf23fe8b9b/340_2024_8280_Fig19_HTML.gif?></graphic></fig></p><p id="Par47">For the CFU detection [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR133">133</xref>], as shown in Fig. <xref rid="Fig19" ref-type="fig">19</xref>a, after the sample is prepared by inoculating bacteria on a chromogenic agar plate, it is positioned on a customized lens-free [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR17">17</xref>, <xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR136">136</xref>] holographic microscopy device for time-lapse imaging which utilized a digital in-line holographic microscopy configuration. The sample is illuminated by a coherent laser source, and the resulting holograms are scanned across the entire sample plate by a complementary metal–oxide–semiconductor (CMOS) sensor. These captured time-lapse holograms are digitally stitched and co-registered across various timestamps to mitigate the effects of random shifts in the mechanical scanning process, and digitally reconstructed to retrieve both the amplitude and phase channels of the observed sample plate. Subsequently, a differential analysis-based image processing algorithm is employed to select colony candidates. These candidates are then fed into a CFU detection neural network to identify true colonies from non-colony candidates (e.g., bubbles, dust and other spatial artifacts). Following this, a CFU classification neural network is subsequently employed to classify true colonies identified by the CFU detection network into their specific species. Note that the CMOS image sensor in this workflow can also be replaced by a thin-film-transistor (TFT) image sensor with a much larger imaging field-of-view (FOV) of ∼ 7–10 cm<sup>2</sup> [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR134">134</xref>]. In this case, the whole FOV of the sample plate can be captured in a single shot using the TFT image sensor and the obtained holograms are inherently registered across all the timestamps, eliminating the need for mechanical scanning, image stitching, and image registration steps that are used in the CMOS sensor-based system.</p><p id="Par48">For the PFU detection [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR135">135</xref>], as shown in Fig. <xref rid="Fig19" ref-type="fig">19</xref>b, the process of hologram capture and image preprocessing are similar to those used in the CFU detection system. However, the candidate selection and identification procedures are not employed in the PFU detection task. Instead, the reconstructed time-lapse phase images of the whole test well are directly converted into a PFU probability map by applying a PFU detection neural network to the whole well image. This PFU probability map is further converted to a binary detection mask after thresholding by 0.5, revealing the sizes and locations of the detected PFUs at a given time point. The neural networks employed in these studies utilized a DenseNet architecture [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR137">137</xref>], with 2D convolutional layers replaced by Pseudo3D convolutional blocks [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR138">138</xref>] to better accommodate time-lapse image sequences. Nonetheless, the network structures suitable for similar work can be changed to more advanced architectures to meet the specific requirements of different detection targets.</p></sec><sec id="Sec45"><title>Results</title><p id="Par49">Following the workflows described above, the presented CFU detection system based on the CMOS image sensor showcased its capability to detect ~ 90% of the true colonies within ~ 7.8 h of incubation for <italic toggle="yes">Escherichia col</italic>i (<italic toggle="yes">E. coli</italic>), ~ 7.0 h for <italic toggle="yes">Klebsiella pneumoniae </italic>(<italic toggle="yes">K. pneumoniae</italic>), and ~ 9.8 h for <italic toggle="yes">Klebsiella aerogenes</italic> (<italic toggle="yes">K. aerogenes</italic>) when tested on 336, 339, and 280 colonies for <italic toggle="yes">E. coli</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">K. pneumoniae</italic>, and <italic toggle="yes">K. aerogenes</italic>, respectively. Compared to the gold-standard Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) approved culture-based methods (requiring > 24 h of incubation), this system achieved time savings of > 12 h [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR133">133</xref>]. As for the TFT sensor-based CFU detection system with simplified hardware and software design [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR134">134</xref>], its detection time was slightly longer compared to the CMOS image sensor-based system, attributed to the larger pixel size of the TFT sensor (~ 321 μm). When tested on 85 <italic toggle="yes">E. coli</italic> colonies, 114 <italic toggle="yes">K. pneumoniae</italic>, and 66 <italic toggle="yes">Citrobacter</italic> colonies, this TFT sensor-based CFU detection system achieved ~ 90% detection rate within ~ 8.0 h for <italic toggle="yes">E. coli</italic>, ~ 7.7 h of incubation for <italic toggle="yes">K. pneumoniae</italic>, and ~ 9.0 h for <italic toggle="yes">Citrobacter</italic>.</p><p id="Par50">Regarding the automated colony classification task, the CMOS sensor-based CFU detection system correctly classified ~ 80% of all the colonies into their species within ~ 8.0 h, ~ 7.6 h, and ~ 12.0 h for <italic toggle="yes">E. coli</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">K. pneumoniae</italic>, and <italic toggle="yes">K. aerogenes</italic>, respectively. In contrast, the TFT sensor-based CFU system was able to classify the detected colonies into either <italic toggle="yes">E. coli</italic> or non-<italic toggle="yes">E. coli</italic> coliforms (<italic toggle="yes">K. pneumoniae </italic>and <italic toggle="yes">Citrobacter</italic>) with an accuracy of > 85% within ~ 11.3 h for <italic toggle="yes">E. coli</italic>, ~ 10.3 h for <italic toggle="yes">K. pneumoniae</italic>, and ~ 13.0 h for <italic toggle="yes">Citrobacter</italic>.</p><p id="Par51">Regarding the PFU detection system, when evaluated on vesicular stomatitis virus (VSV) plates (containing a total of 335 VSV PFUs and five negative control wells), the presented PFU detection system was able to detect 90.3% of VSV PFUs at 17 h, reducing the detection time by > 24 h compared to the traditional viral plaque assays that need 48 h of incubation, followed by chemical staining—which was eliminated through the label-free holographic imaging of the plaque assay. Moreover, after simple transfer learning, this method was demonstrated to successfully generalize to new types of viruses, i.e., herpes simplex virus type 1 (HSV-1) and encephalomyocarditis virus (EMCV). When blindly tested on 6-well plates (containing 214 HSV-1 PFUs and two negative control wells), it achieved a 90.4% HSV-1 detection rate at 72 h, marking a 48 h reduction compared to the traditional 120-h HSV-1 plaque assay. For EMCV, a detection rate of 90.8% was obtained at 52 h of incubation when tested on 6-well plates (containing 249 EMCV PFUs and two negative control wells), achieving 20 h of time-saving compared to the traditional 72-h EMCV plaque assay. Notably, across all detection time points, there were no false positives detected for all the test wells.</p></sec><sec id="Sec46"><title>Conclusion and future perspectives</title><p id="Par52">By leveraging deep learning and holography, the CFU and PFU detection systems discussed in this chapter achieved significant time savings compared to their gold-standard methods. The entire detection process was fully automated and performed in a label-free manner—without the use of any staining chemicals. We believe these automated, label-free systems are not only advantageous for rapid on-site detection but also hold promise in accelerating bacterial and virological research, potentially facilitating the development of antibiotics, vaccines, and antiviral medications.</p></sec></sec><sec id="Sec47"><title>Accelerating computer-generated holography with sparse signal models (David Blinder, Tobias Birnbaum, Peter Schelkens)</title><sec id="Sec48"><title>Background</title><p id="Par53">Computer-generated holography (CGH) comprises many techniques to simulate light diffraction for holography numerically. CGH has many applications for holographic microscopy and tomography [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR22">22</xref>], display technology [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR139">139</xref>], and especially for computational imaging [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR140">140</xref>]. CGH is computationally costly because of the properties of diffraction: every point in the imaged or rendered scene will emit waves that can affect all hologram pixels. That is why a multitude of algorithms have been developed to accelerate and accurately approximate these calculations [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR141">141</xref>].</p><p id="Par54">One particular set of techniques of interest is <italic toggle="yes">sparse CGH algorithms</italic>. These encode the wavefield in a well-chosen transform space where the holographic signals to be computed are sparse; namely, they only require a small number of coefficient updates to be accurate. That way, diffraction calculations can be done much faster, as only a fraction of the total coefficients will be updated. Examples include the use of the sparse FFT [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR142">142</xref>], wavefront recording planes that express zone plate signals in planes close to the virtual object, resulting in limited spatial support, and coefficient-shrinking methods such as WASABI relying on wavelets [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR143">143</xref>].</p><p id="Par55">A transform that has been especially effective in representing holographic signals is the Short-time Fourier transform (STFT). Unlike the standard Fourier transform, the STFT determines the frequency components of localized signal sections as it changes over time (or space). One important reason for its effectiveness in holography is that the impulse response of the diffraction operator is highly sparse in phase space, expressible as a curve in time–frequency space [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR144">144</xref>]. This has shown to be effective for STFT-based CGH with coefficient shrinking [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR144">144</xref>] and the use of phase-added stereograms [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR145">145</xref>, <xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR146">146</xref>].</p><p id="Par56">Recently, the Fresnel diffraction operator itself was accelerated using Gabor frames, relying on the STFT [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR147">147</xref>]. This resulted in a novel Fresnel diffraction algorithm with linear time complexity that needs no zero-padding and can be used for any propagation distance.</p></sec><sec id="Sec49"><title>Methodology</title><p id="Par57">The Fresnel diffraction operator expresses light propagation from a plane z = z<sub>1</sub> to z = z<sub>2</sub> by<disp-formula id="Equ4"><label>4</label><alternatives><tex-math id="M149"><?equation-image-name M149.gif?><?equation-image-status READY?><?equation-image-md5 85dcb12dbe1fc8c993476b4f9bddcb40?><?equation-image-cloudpmc-urn urn:cdn:blobs/9a7a/11362238/85dcb12dbe1f/M149.gif?>\documentclass[12pt]{minimal}

The Gabor coefficients can be processed with the chirplet mapping, and transformed back to obtain the propagated hologram</p></caption><graphic xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" id="MO20" position="float" orientation="portrait" xlink:href="340_2024_8280_Fig20_HTML.jpg"><?image-name 340_2024_8280_Fig20_HTML.jpg?><?image-size 34006?><?image-md5 984270f78c9d7f3866450686ede3998e?><?image-image-server-status LOAD_COMPLETED?><?image-original-height 406?><?image-original-width 1824?><?image-scaled-height 162?><?image-scaled-width 729?><?image-cloudpmc-urn urn:cdn:blobs/9a7a/11362238/984270f78c9d/340_2024_8280_Fig20_HTML.jpg?><?thumb-name 340_2024_8280_Fig20_HTML.gif?><?thumb-size 3967?><?thumb-md5 210ef6552f7860ae916363e7b5e19d9e?><?thumb-image-server-status NEVER_LOAD?><?thumb-scaled-height 45?><?thumb-scaled-width 200?><?thumb-cloudpmc-urn urn:cdn:blobs/9a7a/11362238/210ef6552f78/340_2024_8280_Fig20_HTML.gif?></graphic></fig></p></sec><sec id="Sec50"><title>Results</title><p id="Par65">Because of the sparsity of chirplets for holograms, each input Gabor coefficient will only significantly affect a small number of output Gabor coefficients, no matter the distance <italic toggle="yes">d</italic>. Therefore, only a few coefficients need updating while maintaining high accuracy. Combined with the fact that the computational complexity of the Gabor transform is linear as a function of the number of samples, this results in an <italic toggle="yes">O(n)</italic> Fresnel diffraction algorithm.</p><p id="Par66">We calculated a 1024 × 1024-pixel hologram with a pixel pitch of 4 μm, distance d = 5 cm, and a wavelength λ = 633 nm, cf. Fig. <xref rid="Fig21" ref-type="fig">21</xref>. Using a sheared input coefficient neighborhood with a radius of 5 of input coefficients per output coefficient, we obtain a PSNR of 68.3 dB w.r.t. the reference reconstruction. Preliminary experiments on a C +  + /CUDA implementation give a speedup of about 2 to 4 on a 2048 × 2048-pixel hologram compared to FFT-based Fresnel diffraction [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR149">149</xref>]. The sparsity factor can be chosen to trade off accuracy and speed.<fig id="Fig21" position="float" orientation="portrait"><label>Fig. 21</label><caption><p>Side-by-side comparison of an example hologram propagated with different algorithms, at <italic toggle="yes">d</italic> = 5 mm. <bold>a</bold> The input hologram, followed by multiple reconstructions, using <bold>b</bold> the spatial domain method, <bold>c</bold> the proposed Gabor domain method and <bold>d</bold> the frequency domain method. The proposed Gabor technique appears to be visually identical to the reference spatial and frequency domain algorithms</p></caption><graphic xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" id="MO21" position="float" orientation="portrait" xlink:href="340_2024_8280_Fig21_HTML.jpg"><?image-name 340_2024_8280_Fig21_HTML.jpg?><?image-size 82131?><?image-md5 153222a575cf175041ce1b10846f76ae?><?image-image-server-status LOAD_COMPLETED?><?image-original-height 528?><?image-original-width 1959?><?image-scaled-height 211?><?image-scaled-width 783?><?image-cloudpmc-urn urn:cdn:blobs/9a7a/11362238/153222a575cf/340_2024_8280_Fig21_HTML.jpg?><?thumb-name 340_2024_8280_Fig21_HTML.gif?><?thumb-size 6026?><?thumb-md5 a4f6af2f0b561823a46d5d4a42645b5d?><?thumb-image-server-status NEVER_LOAD?><?thumb-scaled-height 54?><?thumb-scaled-width 200?><?thumb-cloudpmc-urn urn:cdn:blobs/9a7a/11362238/a4f6af2f0b56/340_2024_8280_Fig21_HTML.gif?></graphic></fig></p></sec><sec id="Sec51"><title>Conclusion and future perspectives</title><p id="Par67">We have combined two of Dennis Gabor’s inventions, holography, and the Gabor transform, creating a novel method for numerical Fresnel diffraction. It is a new, distinct mathematical way to express discrete Fresnel diffraction with multiple algorithmic benefits. The method requires no zero-padding, poses no limits on the distance <italic toggle="yes">d</italic> and inherently supports off-axis propagation and changes in pixel pitch or resolution. Its sparsity enables a linear complexity algorithm implementation. We plan to investigate these matters and perform detailed experiments in future work. This novel propagation technique may serve as a basis for more efficient and flexible propagation operators for various applications in computational imaging with diffraction.</p></sec></sec><sec id="Sec52"><title>Layer-based hologram calculations: practical implementations (Tomoyoshi Shimobaba)</title><sec id="Sec53"><title>Background</title><p id="Par68">Holographic displays have attracted significant attention as one of the most promising technologies for three-dimensional (3D) displays. They require optical systems capable of rendering holograms with a large spatial bandwidth, in addition to algorithms and computational hardware that can efficiently compute these holograms at high speeds [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR139">139</xref>]. Computational algorithms designed for hologram generation can be broadly categorized into several methods, including point cloud, polygon, layer, light field, and deep learning-based approaches. Each method has its own set of advantages and disadvantages, and currently, there is no universally perfect method identified. In this context, we focus on the layer method.</p><p id="Par69">The layer method computes holograms from a 3D scene represented by an RGB image and a depth image (RGB-D image). Depth cameras, such as the Kinect, are now readily available for capturing RGB-D images. Alternatively, RGB-D images can be obtained from computer graphics generated using 3D graphics libraries such as OpenGL. A prototype of a holographic near-eye display utilizing RGB-D images has been successfully developed and has effectively presented 3D images to viewers without causing discomfort [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR150">150</xref>]. The layer method decomposes a 3D scene into multiple 2D images (referred to as layers) or point clouds, from which holograms can be computed [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR151">151</xref>]. This chapter provides a detailed exposition of the layer method.</p></sec><sec id="Sec54"><title>Methodology</title><p id="Par70">A schematic of the hologram computation using the layer method is presented in Fig. <xref rid="Fig22" ref-type="fig">22</xref>, wherein an example of RGB and depth images is illustrated. Figure <xref rid="Fig22" ref-type="fig">22</xref>b details the process of computing a layer hologram through diffraction calculations. This RGB-D image serves as the basis for decomposing the 3D scene into multiple layers. The light waves emitted from each of these layers are individually computed and subsequently combined on the hologram, resulting in the final hologram [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR152">152</xref>]. To expedite the computation, a virtual plane, known as the wavefront recording plane (WRP), is positioned in close proximity to the point cloud. The light waves are subsequently recorded on the WRP, denoted as <italic toggle="yes">w</italic>(<italic toggle="yes">x</italic>), using Eq. (<xref rid="Equ12" ref-type="disp-formula">12</xref>) [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR156">156</xref>, <xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR157">157</xref>]. Once all the object point information is recorded on the WRP, the hologram can be generated by performing a diffraction calculation from the WRP to the hologram. Layer images often exhibit sparsity. In such instances, using FFTs in Eq. (<xref rid="Equ10" ref-type="disp-formula">10</xref>) for calculations would be less efficient owing to the presence of layers containing many zeros. If each layer is sparse, it would be more efficient to calculate the hologram by using Eq. (<xref rid="Equ12" ref-type="disp-formula">12</xref>). The introduction of multiple WRPs is a possibility, and optimal values for the number and placement of these WRPs exist [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR158">158</xref>].</p><p id="Par76">Holograms obtained using Eqs. (<xref rid="Equ10" ref-type="disp-formula">10</xref>) and (<xref rid="Equ12" ref-type="disp-formula">12</xref>) are inherently complex-valued. Typical spatial light modulators (SLMs) are capable of performing either amplitude or phase modulation. Therefore, complex holograms need to be converted into a format suitable for SLMs. In the case of amplitude modulation SLMs, methods are employed that either directly extract the real part of the complex hologram to produce an amplitude hologram or utilize techniques such as single sideband and half-zone plate processing to achieve a complex hologram even when using amplitude modulation SLMs [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR159">159</xref>, <xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR160">160</xref>]. For phase modulation SLMs, complex holograms are transformed into phase-only holograms through methods such as double phase hologram [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR161">161</xref>, <xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR162">162</xref>], error diffusion method [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR163">163</xref>], binary amplitude encoding [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR164">164</xref>], and bleached hologram [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR165">165</xref>].</p></sec><sec id="Sec55"><title>Results</title><p id="Par77">The results of computing the layer hologram from the RGB-D image in Fig. <xref rid="Fig22" ref-type="fig">22</xref>a using Eq. (<xref rid="Equ10" ref-type="disp-formula">10</xref>) are displayed in Fig. <xref rid="Fig23" ref-type="fig">23</xref>. For these diffraction calculations, the angular spectrum method was applied [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR166">166</xref>]. The following parameters were used: a wavelength of 532 nm, a minimum distance of 50 mm between the hologram and the 3D scene, a pixel pitch of 3.74 µm, a thickness of 5 mm for the 3D scene (where a zero-pixel value in the depth image corresponds to a distance of 50 mm from the hologram, and a pixel value of 255 represents a distance of 55 mm), and a total of 32 layers.<fig id="Fig23" position="float" orientation="portrait"><label>Fig. 23</label><caption><p>Layer holograms and reproduced images. <bold>a</bold> Hologram using compensation phase, <bold>b</bold> reproduced image focused on standlight, <bold>c</bold> reproduced image focused on shelf, <bold>d</bold> hologram using random phase, <bold>e</bold> reproduced image focused on standlight, <bold>f</bold> reproduced image focused on shelf. The contrast and brightness of each reproduced image were adjusted for ease of viewing</p></caption><graphic xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" id="MO23" position="float" orientation="portrait" xlink:href="340_2024_8280_Fig23_HTML.jpg"><?image-name 340_2024_8280_Fig23_HTML.jpg?><?image-size 184436?><?image-md5 d7fef19d8c87096c3b38bfd305cb7770?><?image-image-server-status LOAD_COMPLETED?><?image-original-height 990?><?image-original-width 1497?><?image-scaled-height 495?><?image-scaled-width 748?><?image-cloudpmc-urn urn:cdn:blobs/9a7a/11362238/d7fef19d8c87/340_2024_8280_Fig23_HTML.jpg?><?thumb-name 340_2024_8280_Fig23_HTML.gif?><?thumb-size 9626?><?thumb-md5 94a10d9a5ea467f779f116e654e86a73?><?thumb-image-server-status NEVER_LOAD?><?thumb-scaled-height 79?><?thumb-scaled-width 120?><?thumb-cloudpmc-urn urn:cdn:blobs/9a7a/11362238/94a10d9a5ea4/340_2024_8280_Fig23_HTML.gif?></graphic></fig></p><p id="Par78">Figure <xref rid="Fig23" ref-type="fig">23</xref>a shows the hologram utilizing the compensation phase for <italic toggle="yes">ψ(x)</italic> is presented. Further, Fig. <xref rid="Fig23" ref-type="fig">23</xref>b and c show the reproduced images derived from the hologram. Figure <xref rid="Fig23" ref-type="fig">23</xref>b displays the reproduced image with a focus on the standlight, while Fig. <xref rid="Fig23" ref-type="fig">23</xref>c exhibits the reproduced image with emphasis on the shelf. Figure <xref rid="Fig23" ref-type="fig">23</xref>d illustrates the hologram created using the random phase for <italic toggle="yes">ψ(x)</italic>. Correspondingly, Fig. <xref rid="Fig23" ref-type="fig">23</xref>e and f reveal the reproduced images from the hologram, with a specific focus on the standlight and the shelf, respectively. Notably, the reproduced image originating from the hologram utilizing the compensation phase manifests a deep depth of field, whereas the reproduced image obtained from the hologram using the random phase exhibits a shallow depth of field. Furthermore, the reproduced image of the random phase hologram displays a pronounced presence of speckle noise.</p></sec><sec id="Sec56"><title>Conclusion and future perspectives</title><p id="Par79">This section describes the calculation of layer holograms, and the Python code with accompanying comments can be found in the supplementary material. The layer holograms discussed here are commonly applied in near-eye holographic displays [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR150">150</xref>]. However, this method may not be suitable for holographic displays with broad viewing angles and expansive fields of view, where the observer's eye position can be freely adjusted [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR167">167</xref>]. For such holographic displays, an alternative approach involves calculating layer holograms using multi-view images in conjunction with depth images [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR168">168</xref>]. Many hologram computations using deep learning methods also involve inferring layer holograms from RGB-D images. The layer hologram calculations presented in this chapter, serve a valuable purpose in generating training datasets for deep learning. Additionally, while layer holograms derived through deep learning may face challenges in achieving deep-depth reproduction images [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR169">169</xref>], the computational approach introduced in this chapter allows for greater flexibility in setting the depth parameter. Commented Python code for implementing layer hologram calculation is given in the supplementary materials S9.</p></sec></sec><sec id="Sec57"><title>Learned compressive holography (Vladislav Kravets and Adrian Stern)</title><sec id="Sec58"><title>Background</title><p id="Par80">In [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR170">170</xref>] we introduced Compressive Fresnel Holography (CFH)—a technique that uses only a small subset of samples of the hologram to capture the object’s three-dimensional information. The CFH was built upon the Compressive Sensing (CS) [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR171">171</xref>–<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR173">173</xref>] theory, which states that objects that are sparse or have a sparse representation in some mathematical domain can be economically sampled and reconstructed by employing an appropriate sampling scheme and reconstruction algorithm. Using this technique, a compression ratio of up to 12.5:1 was demonstrated in [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR170">170</xref>] for Fresnel coherent digital holography. The method was extended for incoherent holography in [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR174">174</xref>, <xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR175">175</xref>] facilitating the sensing effort by an order of magnitude. Theoretical guarantees for CFH were derived in [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR176">176</xref>], and comprehensive sampling conditions are summarized in Chapter 9 in [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR173">173</xref>].</p><p id="Par81">The CS theory considers a linear sensing model described as <inline-formula id="IEq100"><alternatives><tex-math id="M223"><?equation-image-name M223.gif?><?equation-image-status READY?><?equation-image-md5 50d616486edf31f20a1bc87b17bb6124?><?equation-image-cloudpmc-urn urn:cdn:blobs/9a7a/11362238/50d616486edf/M223.gif?>\documentclass[12pt]{minimal}

The RM sensing matrix is an M by N random matrix with entries commonly drawn from a sub-Gaussian distribution (e.g., Gaussian Bernoulli, etc.). The best-known representative of PRE is the Random Partial Fourier (RPF) sensing matrix, which is constructed by randomly picking out M rows from a Fourier Basis. The CFH sensing model relates to this method, suggesting randomly sampling only <italic toggle="yes">M</italic> samples from a full Fresnel transformation ensemble, as we demonstrated in [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR170">170</xref>]. We further have shown that it is advantageous to sample Fresnel holograms randomly according to a non-uniform pattern [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR170">170</xref>]. Similar non-uniform CS sampling was also studied for other CS settings (e.g., [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR177">177</xref>, <xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR178">178</xref>]) using theoretical analysis of the sensing matrix. In this chapter, we present a data-driven deep learning method to determine the optimal random-like sampling. We apply the recently introduced LPTnet [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR179">179</xref>] to choose the optimal Fresnel samples and to reconstruct the object from the CS samples. LPTnet was demonstrated in [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR179">179</xref>] to push the classical CS limits by almost two orders of magnitudes when applied to regular 2D imaging. Here, we demonstrate its usefulness for CFH.</p><p id="Par82">LPTnet is an innovative CS framework that utilizes end-to-end Deep Learning (DL) for jointly optimizing the sensing process and the CS reconstruction algorithm. Unlike traditional CS methods that often rely on random sampling techniques, LPTnet intelligently selects optimal samples from a predetermined transformation ensemble using deep learning. Figure <xref rid="Fig1" ref-type="fig">1</xref> shows a simplified scheme of LPTNet. Notice that each case has its own Fresnel transformation ensemble, <inline-formula id="IEq122"><alternatives><tex-math id="M269"><?equation-image-name M269.gif?><?equation-image-status READY?><?equation-image-md5 cfa2cc33b7637c1cecbee5236761b6aa?><?equation-image-cloudpmc-urn urn:cdn:blobs/9a7a/11362238/cfa2cc33b763/M269.gif?>\documentclass[12pt]{minimal}

				\begin{document}$${{\varvec{\Phi}}}^{FST}={{\varvec{\Phi}}}^{FST}\left(z,\frac{M}{N}\right)$$\end{document}</tex-math><mml:math xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" id="M270"><mml:mrow><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">Φ</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="italic">FST</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="bold">Φ</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi mathvariant="italic">FST</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mfenced close=")" open="("><mml:mi>z</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mfrac><mml:mi>M</mml:mi><mml:mi>N</mml:mi></mml:mfrac></mml:mfenced></mml:mrow></mml:math><inline-graphic xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" xlink:href="340_2024_8280_Article_IEq122.gif"><?image-name 340_2024_8280_Article_IEq122.gif?><?image-size 739?><?image-md5 2670b67e41d3fa65b3aa4bffa769be73?><?image-image-server-status NEVER_LOAD?><?image-scaled-height 23?><?image-scaled-width 154?><?image-cloudpmc-urn urn:cdn:blobs/9a7a/11362238/2670b67e41d3/340_2024_8280_Article_IEq122.gif?><?thumb-name 340_2024_8280_Article_IEq122.gif?><?thumb-size 739?><?thumb-md5 2670b67e41d3fa65b3aa4bffa769be73?><?thumb-image-server-status NEVER_LOAD?><?thumb-scaled-height 23?><?thumb-scaled-width 154?><?thumb-cloudpmc-urn urn:cdn:blobs/9a7a/11362238/2670b67e41d3/340_2024_8280_Article_IEq122.gif?></inline-graphic></alternatives></inline-formula>, therefore LPTnet finds an appropriate sampling map. It can be seen that for short distances, where the Fresnel transformation is not much different from that of the object, the optimal sampling pattern is uniformly random, which is in agreement with the universal CS oracles that do not employ learning tools. However, as the field propagates, the sampling pattern becomes patterned. Figure <xref rid="Fig25" ref-type="fig">25</xref>b (center and bottom) demonstrates the image reconstructions of Augustin-Jean Fresnel portrait (Fig. <xref rid="Fig25" ref-type="fig">25</xref>b) from as few as <italic toggle="yes">M</italic> = 200 and <italic toggle="yes">M</italic> = 500 samples for <italic toggle="yes">z</italic> = 25 mm for <italic toggle="yes">z</italic> = 192 mm.</p></sec><sec id="Sec61"><title>Conclusion and future perspectives</title><p id="Par87">In this study, we introduced Learned Compressive Holography—a method that determines the optimal hologram sampling pattern according to the particular imaging conditions. For this purpose, we utilized the LPTnet framework, which jointly optimizes the sampling pattern and a reconstitution deep neural network via a learning process. We have shown that applying the LPTnet framework to compressive Fresnel holography can enhance image reconstruction from a reduced number of samples. This approach, which aligns with CS principles, has proven effective in reconstructing detailed images with fewer resources. The use of LPTnet to select optimal samples from the Fresnel transform is a notable improvement over traditional random sampling methods. Our results show the potential of this method for efficiently handling sparse data. In the future, we will investigate the use of CFH for other types of coherent and incoherent holography methods.</p></sec></sec><sec id="Sec62"><title>Computational optical phase imaging: from digital holographic interferometry to intensity diffraction tomography (Shun Zhou, Jiaji Li, Jiasong Sun, Qian Chen, and Chao Zuo)</title><sec id="Sec63"><title>Background</title><p id="Par88">One of the prominent challenges encountered in optical microscopy relates to contrast enhancement. Traditional microscopy relies on the mechanism of intensity-based detection, which necessitates the use of staining agents to visualize transparent specimens, such as biological cells. On the contrary, label-free microscopy has emerged as an ideal method for exploring the physiological activities and long-term dynamic processes of living cells. In 1932, Zernike introduced the technique of phase contrast microscope which utilizes the principle of aperture modulation and spatial filtering, significantly enhancing the contrast for transparent specimens [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR180">180</xref>]. Nevertheless, while this phase imaging method excels in two-dimensional (2D) qualitative visualization, it has not yet been successfully extended to three-dimensional (3D) quantitative measurements.</p><p id="Par89">Inspired by Zernike’s concepts, various innovative label-free microscopic techniques gradually emerged, among which quantitative phase imaging (QPI) is considered one of the most promising approaches [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR181">181</xref>]. In particular, 3D optical diffraction tomography (ODT) can be realized by combining QPI with computed tomography, providing true 3D refractive index (RI) distribution inside the sample. The realization of ODT is of great significance for revealing the intrinsic mechanisms of cell biology and pathophysiology. Unfortunately, the measurements of the quantitative phase cannot get rid of laser and optical interference for over half a century. Inherent defects of interferometric detection, such as complex interference devices, speckle noise, and coherent diffraction limit have not been fundamentally resolved for a long time, and these enduring obstacles hinder the widespread applications and long-term future development of interferometric holography in the field of biological imaging.</p><p id="Par90">Over the past decade, we have spearheaded research in computational optical phase imaging domestically and also exerted influence internationally. We are primarily focusing on the theory development of generalized phase definition under partially coherent light field and phase transfer function (PTF), and the technique advances of spatial bandwidth product (SBP) enhancement and intensity diffraction tomography. These efforts contribute to the development of innovative theories and methods for non-interferometric quantitative phase and diffraction tomographic imaging.</p></sec><sec id="Sec64"><title>Methodology and results</title><sec id="Sec65"><title>From fully coherent field to partially coherent field</title><p id="Par91">The scalar diffraction theory proposed by Huygen is sufficient to accurately describe the propagation of the light field in free space and its complex amplitude distribution on an arbitrary plane for the case of a fully coherent illumination light field. The corresponding inverse problem can be solved iteratively by phase retrieval methods such as GS, hybrid input–output algorithm (HIO), or directly by the transport of intensity equation (TIE) under the paraxial approximation [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR182">182</xref>]. It is worth noting that the intensity forward models relied upon by these phase retrieval techniques assume of fully coherent illumination. However, the partially coherent fields exhibit statistical properties with random fluctuations and cannot be fully described by the 2D complex amplitude, so there is no clear phase definition. To address the above issues, as depicted in Fig. <xref rid="Fig26" ref-type="fig">26</xref>, we established the generalized TIE and provided a strict definition of the generalized phase under partially coherent field based on the Wigner distribution function in phase space [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR183">183</xref>]. The generalized phase serves as a scalar potential function, with its gradient representing the first-order conditional frequency moment of the Wigner distribution function under the partially coherent field, thus extending the well-posedness of TIE from the fully coherent wavefield to the wavefield in any coherent state. Based on Poynting's theorem in the unbounded space, we have strictly proven the existence and uniqueness of the solution to the equation under non-homogeneous Neumann boundary conditions [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR184">184</xref>]. This achievement effectively addresses a long-standing theoretical problem of obtaining an exact solution to TIE [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR185">185</xref>], which lays a theoretical foundation for QPI from interference to non-interference and from fully coherent illumination to partially coherent illumination.<fig id="Fig26" position="float" orientation="portrait"><label>Fig. 26</label><caption><p>Generalized TIE and generalized phase under partially coherent field derived from the Wigner distribution function in phase space</p></caption><graphic xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" id="MO26" position="float" orientation="portrait" xlink:href="340_2024_8280_Fig26_HTML.jpg"><?image-name 340_2024_8280_Fig26_HTML.jpg?><?image-size 73431?><?image-md5 7d207170b95875a52f00a96597e6ab39?><?image-image-server-status LOAD_COMPLETED?><?image-original-height 732?><?image-original-width 1500?><?image-scaled-height 366?><?image-scaled-width 750?><?image-cloudpmc-urn urn:cdn:blobs/9a7a/11362238/7d207170b958/340_2024_8280_Fig26_HTML.jpg?><?thumb-name 340_2024_8280_Fig26_HTML.gif?><?thumb-size 6138?><?thumb-md5 88d66cc6f6601356a12eb5480b49e48d?><?thumb-image-server-status NEVER_LOAD?><?thumb-scaled-height 80?><?thumb-scaled-width 163?><?thumb-cloudpmc-urn urn:cdn:blobs/9a7a/11362238/88d66cc6f660/340_2024_8280_Fig26_HTML.gif?></graphic></fig></p></sec><sec id="Sec66"><title>From coherent diffraction limit to incoherent diffraction limit</title><p id="Par92">Extending QPI technique from fully coherent to partially coherent illumination also offers the benefit of enhancing imaging resolution thanks to the inherent synthetic aperture. Classical Fourier optics theory reveals that the incoherent optical transfer function (OTF) is the normalized autocorrelation of the coherent transfer function (also known as pupil function), resulting in a cutoff frequency twice that of the coherent diffraction limit. However, this conclusion cannot quantitatively describe the phase imaging characteristics under partially coherent illumination that lies between fully coherent and incoherent. More importantly, as coherence decreases, the incoherent imaging system degrades to a linear system of intensity and loses its capability to image phase objects. To address these challenges, we have developed the PTF theory under partially coherent illumination by separating the contribution of the specimen and system within the image formation process [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR186">186</xref>] , providing a more nuanced understanding of how these factors interact to produce the final image. The equation and visual representations of the PTF, including 2D cross-sectional illustration and line profile, are shown in Fig. <xref rid="Fig27" ref-type="fig">27</xref>a. These illustrations provide a clear visual explanation of imaging resolution enhancement through the use of partially coherent illumination. Moreover, the imaginary part of the weak object transfer function for various coherent parameters s (the ratio of illumination NA to objective NA) and defocus distances are illustrated in Fig. <xref rid="Fig27" ref-type="fig">27</xref>b. The PTF theory not only reveals the trade-off between cutoff frequency and response amplitude under traditional circular illumination apertures but also demonstrates that annular illumination matching the objective NA effectively expands the support domain up to twice the cutoff frequency corresponding to the objective NA, while maintaining optimal response [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR187">187</xref>, <xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR188">188</xref>] . Based on this, we have proposed a transport-of-intensity QPI method that utilizes NA-matched annular illumination, effectively extending the imaging resolution from the coherent diffraction limit to the incoherent diffraction limit. The corresponding experimental setup is depicted in Fig. <xref rid="Fig27" ref-type="fig">27</xref>c. The effectiveness of our proposed approach is exemplified by the imaging of subcellular structures within buccal epithelial cells. Figure <xref rid="Fig27" ref-type="fig">27</xref>c demonstrates the multi-mode imaging results, encompassing quantitative phase, phase contrast, differential interference contrast (DIC), and pseudo-color 3D rendering. These collectively underscore the superior imaging capability of our method in revealing intricate cellular details that were previously inaccessible with traditional imaging techniques.<fig id="Fig27" position="float" orientation="portrait"><label>Fig. 27</label><caption><p>QPI under partially coherent illumination. <bold>a</bold> Partially coherent phase transfer function. <bold>b</bold> The imaginary part of weak object transfer function for various coherent parameters and defocus distances. <bold>c</bold> High-resolution imaging of buccal epithelial cells based on transport-of-intensity quantitative phase microscopy with annular illumination</p></caption><graphic xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" id="MO27" position="float" orientation="portrait" xlink:href="340_2024_8280_Fig27_HTML.jpg"><?image-name 340_2024_8280_Fig27_HTML.jpg?><?image-size 162302?><?image-md5 f443915dc63d1a64bf5db72b0879d54d?><?image-image-server-status LOAD_COMPLETED?><?image-original-height 1423?><?image-original-width 1804?><?image-scaled-height 569?><?image-scaled-width 721?><?image-cloudpmc-urn urn:cdn:blobs/9a7a/11362238/f443915dc63d/340_2024_8280_Fig27_HTML.jpg?><?thumb-name 340_2024_8280_Fig27_HTML.gif?><?thumb-size 6556?><?thumb-md5 0aa394183370d6951dcac85bad1a495a?><?thumb-image-server-status NEVER_LOAD?><?thumb-scaled-height 80?><?thumb-scaled-width 101?><?thumb-cloudpmc-urn urn:cdn:blobs/9a7a/11362238/0aa394183370/340_2024_8280_Fig27_HTML.gif?></graphic></fig></p></sec><sec id="Sec67"><title>From defocus phase reconstruction to ptychographic bandwidth expansion</title><p id="Par93">To achieve QPI, it is crucial to introduce imaginary components into the complex function of the OTF under partially coherent illumination. In TIE, this is accomplished by introducing defocus into the imaging system (complex pupil function). Another method involves breaking the radial symmetry of the imaging system by employing asymmetric illumination or asymmetric aperture, such as differential phase contrast (DPC) and Fourier ptychographic microscopy (FPM) [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR189">189</xref>]. With this approach, we derived the PTF under asymmetric illumination, as depicted in Fig. <xref rid="Fig28" ref-type="fig">28</xref>a, which reveals the intrinsic relationship between the illumination/detection numerical aperture ratio and the imaging SBP in the FPM. By applying the large illumination NA to a low-magnification objective, the imaging system’s SBP can be expanded by utilizing the multiple differences between the illumination NA and the objective NA [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR190">190</xref>, <xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR191">191</xref>]. In Fig. <xref rid="Fig28" ref-type="fig">28</xref>b, we built an FPM system based on a high-NA programmable condenser, achieving super-resolution and high-throughput imaging with an equivalent NA of 1.6 under the large field of view of a 10 × objective using oil-immersed condenser illumination. Additionally, our research has revealed that FPM is constrained by matched illumination condition and proposed a high-speed FPM approach based on annular illumination, enabling high-speed, long-time, and adaptive-aberration-correction high-throughput phase imaging [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR192">192</xref>, <xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR193">193</xref>], as illustrated in Fig. <xref rid="Fig28" ref-type="fig">28</xref>c.<fig id="Fig28" position="float" orientation="portrait"><label>Fig. 28</label><caption><p>Wide-field, high-resolution FPM. <bold>a</bold> OTF under asymmetric coherent the approaches of TIE and FPM effectively eliminate the defect of QPI based on interference, the persistence of the divide-and-conquer thought of “phase recovery followed by diffraction tomography” still constrains the realization of 3D tomography. In the past five years, our research focus has gradually shifted from phase imaging to diffraction tomography, venturing into a new class of non-interferometric label-free 3D microscopic imaging techniques—intensity diffraction tomography (IDT). IDT incorporates the principles of “phase retrieval from intensity” and “RI reconstruction from phase”, bypassing the intermediate step of “phase measurement”. It allows for the direct reconstruction of 3D RI distribution exclusively using the intensity information generated by illumination angle scanning or axial scanning of the sample. As depicted in Fig. <xref rid="Fig29" ref-type="fig">29</xref>a, IDT can be categorized into two main implementations: transport of intensity diffraction tomography (TIDT) based on axial scanning [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR186">186</xref>, <xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR194">194</xref>] and Fourier ptychographic diffraction tomography (FPDT) based on illumination angle scanning [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR195">195</xref>, <xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR196">196</xref>]. Specifically, TIDT expands the 2D plane intensity transmission of TIE to 3D volume transmission, achieving parallelized coverage of the object's 3D scattering potential spectrum through the use of partially coherent illumination. TIDT first records the intensity image stack of the sample’s scattered field at different axial positions under partially coherent illumination, and then performs 3D deconvolution based on the 3D phase optical transfer function corresponding to the imaging system to obtain the 3D RI distribution information of the sample. This method enables label-free 3D imaging with a lateral resolution of 206 nm and an axial resolution of 520 nm under a high NA oil immersion objective, and the dynamic 3D RI imaging results of HeLa live cells are shown in Fig. <xref rid="Fig29" ref-type="fig">29</xref>b. On the other hand, FPDT expands the 2D plane aperture ptychography of FPM to 3D volume ptychography and establishes the intensity forward model under both bright- and dark-field illumination based on the first-order Born and Rytov approximation, respectively. A 3D spectrum updating model is further built based on the quantitative relationship between the scattering potential of the sample and the recorded intensity. FPDT uses a low-NA objective to acquire a sequence of intensity images corresponding to different illumination angles scanned sequentially with a programmable light-emitting-diode array. Then, this method gradually combines these intensity images into a 3D spectrum of the object using a ptychographic reconstruction algorithm. After the convergence of the algorithm, an inverse Fourier transform is performed to obtain the sample’s 3D RI distribution. By employing high-NA dark-field illumination, FPDT achieves high-throughput label-free 3D diffraction tomography with a lateral resolution of 390 nm and an axial resolution of 899 nm across a 10 × FOV of 1.77 mm<sup>2</sup> and a depth of focus of ~ 20 μm. The high-resolution and large FOV 3D RI imaging results of HeLa cells are shown in Fig. <xref rid="Fig29" ref-type="fig">29</xref>c, which contains nearly 4000 Hela cells. <fig id="Fig29" position="float" orientation="portrait"><label>Fig. 29</label><caption><p>Label-free 3D microscopy based on IDT. <bold>a</bold> Schematic of TIDT and FPDT. <bold>b</bold> Dynamic 3D RI imaging of HeLa live cells using TIDT. <bold>c</bold> High-resolution, large field of view 3D RI imaging of HeLa cells using FPDT</p></caption><graphic xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" id="MO29" position="float" orientation="portrait" xlink:href="340_2024_8280_Fig29_HTML.jpg"><?image-name 340_2024_8280_Fig29_HTML.jpg?><?image-size 125606?><?image-md5 4c4c2462b17912c7da0003248fdccc2e?><?image-image-server-status LOAD_COMPLETED?><?image-original-height 1456?><?image-original-width 2028?><?image-scaled-height 485?><?image-scaled-width 676?><?image-cloudpmc-urn urn:cdn:blobs/9a7a/11362238/4c4c2462b179/340_2024_8280_Fig29_HTML.jpg?><?thumb-name 340_2024_8280_Fig29_HTML.gif?><?thumb-size 15843?><?thumb-md5 e103ce0f9d67052b3379a7bfcc982329?><?thumb-image-server-status NEVER_LOAD?><?thumb-scaled-height 80?><?thumb-scaled-width 111?><?thumb-cloudpmc-urn urn:cdn:blobs/9a7a/11362238/e103ce0f9d67/340_2024_8280_Fig29_HTML.gif?></graphic></fig></p></sec></sec><sec id="Sec69"><title>Conclusion and future perspectives</title><p id="Par95">The emergence of computational optical quantitative phase imaging and intensity diffraction tomography means rigorous coherence and interferometry are no longer prerequisites for QPI and ODT, which marks the great progress of label-free microscopic imaging techniques based on phase detection into a novel stage. And these advancements will open up new possibilities for label-free 3D microscopy and are expected to be widely applied in various biomedicine and life sciences. Nonetheless, these techniques still face a series of ongoing challenges and problems permitting further exploration in the future, including the combination of TIDT and FPDT to break through the limit of matched illumination condition [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR197">197</xref>], the optimization of the forward model for samples with multiple scattering to go beyond the Born and Rytov approximations [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR198">198</xref>], and the suppression of the missing-cone problem in Ewald sphere spectrum to expand the axial support region [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR199">199</xref>]. Furthermore, the potential combination of IDT and 3D super-resolution fluorescence microscopy imaging technique holds promise for opening a new window to observe nanoscale details inside living cells at the single-cell and subcellular levels. The breakthrough brought by computational optical phase imaging might provide more valuable insights into applications such as single-cell morphology and dynamics analyses, cellular interactions, cellular responses, and label-free pathology diagnosis. Detailed insights into computational optical quantitative phase imaging and intensity diffraction tomography, including specific theories and methods, are consolidated in [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR186">186</xref>]. For a deeper comprehension of the MATLAB source codes, readers are encouraged to refer to the details provided in [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR186">186</xref>] and visit <ext-link xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" ext-link-type="uri" xlink:href="https://scilaboratory.com/code.html">https://scilaboratory.com/code.html</ext-link>.</p></sec></sec><sec id="Sec70"><title>Computational hyperspectral quantitative phase imaging from spectrally multiplexed observations (Igor Shevkunov, Vladimir Katkovnik, and Karen Egiazarian)</title><sec id="Sec71"><title>Background</title><p id="Par96">We consider a novel setup and a novel computational algorithm for hyperspectral (HS) QPI from total intensity observations, which are the sums of spectral intensities over a wide spectral range. This setup is explicitly based on computational analysis of the observations and does not require any spectral devices, which makes HS imaging simple. This imaging can be applied to non-invasive and label-free sample observations, which is especially valuable for biological and medical laboratories where dying and labeling might harm a specimen [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR182">182</xref>]. Our HSQPI is an extension of the basic ideas of the phase retrieval techniques [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR200">200</xref>]. Overall, the phase retrieval problems are ill-posed and require multiple diverse observations for high-quality imaging. This kind of diversity can be achieved in different ways: through varying registration distances [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR201">201</xref>], multiple phase encoded apertures [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR202">202</xref>], or sets of wavelengths [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR203">203</xref>]. The latter case provides hyperspectral modality which in turn provides a broadening of the technique with the imaging in a wide spectral range. Typically, spectral observations for phase retrieval are registered for each spectral channel separately, channel-by-channel, which is realized either by sets of narrow-band filters [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR203">203</xref>] or by a tunable light source [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR204">204</xref>]. Contrary to it, we use our recently developed algorithm, named HS Phase Retrival (HSPhR) algorithm [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR205">205</xref>], which provides hyperspectral phase retrieval in parallel for all spectral channels from the spectrally multiplexed observations. The separation of spectral channels is achieved due to modulation encoding phase-masks and the developed HSPhR, including the original spectral proximity operators and complex-domain alternating direction algorithm of multipliers (ADMM) [<xref ref-type="bibr" rid="CR206">206</xref>].</p><p id="Par97">In the considered setup of the HS phase retrieval (see Fig. <xref rid="Fig30" ref-type="fig">30</xref>a), we utilize random phase masks <inline-formula id="IEq123"><alternatives><tex-math id="M271"><?equation-image-name M271.gif?><?equation-image-status READY?><?equation-image-md5 85aa5b741c9cce6445d4267c89dc6529?><?equation-image-cloudpmc-urn urn:cdn:blobs/9a7a/11362238/85aa5b741c9c/M271.gif?>\documentclass[12pt]{minimal}

Further, the light beam propagates freely 2 mm to the registration camera ‘CMOS.’</p><p id="Par100">The SLM parameters were chosen to limit phase range of the object (cameraman image, 64 × 64 pixels) to [0: π] rad in the whole spectral range, this phase distribution for wavelength of 744 nm is shown in Fig. <xref rid="Fig30" ref-type="fig">30</xref>d.
